Thank you, Madam Speaker. I had the opportunity to review thoroughly Bill C-2. I then compared Bill C-2 with the legislation that died on the order paper, Bill C-142, to see what differences there were. I then compared Bill C-2 with the legislation that is currently in operation, the Canadian Aviation Safety Act, and attempted to analyse the differences between these two pieces of legislation with the intention of
April 17, 1989

seeing whether or not the new piece of legislation could be operative.
As I was going through this legislation, my thoughts returned to a time approximately 10 years ago when I was at the University of Windsor in the Faculty of Law. The professors in that faculty instilled in me an interest in statutory law, statutory interpretation and administrative law, and I thank them for that, particularly one of my favourite professors who is now the Dean of Law at McGill University. It is from that perspective that I will make my comments with respect to Bill C-2.
As I was preparing my comments, I found it interesting to read an article in the Saturday, April 15, edition of The Ottawa Citizen in which the Chairman of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, commenting on his annual report, urged Parliament to quickly pass Bill C-2 so that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board will be abolished because the Board is divided. The present Board is made up of nine members appointed by the Governor in Council. As I have stated, I have reviewed the Canadian Aviation Safety Act and I see nothing in that legislation which states that all Board decisions must be unanimous.
In reviewing most Canadian dispute resolution bodies and particularly the appellate court system, I find that these panels usually sit with three, five or nine members. The reason for this is logical and reasonable. Decisions arrived at should be arrived at on the evidence presented and members of a decision-making body may interpret that evidence differently. When decisions are made by these bodies, they are majority decisions based on the evidence presented. If the dissenting members of a panel or bench feel strongly about the issue and want to express their opinions, they usually do so by writing a dissenting opinion and stating their reasons for doing so. This is much the same as what we have seen happen recently with the Canadian Aviation Safety Board with respect to a recent investigation. There was a division of thought between the members of the Board, and as a result, there were dissenting opinions.
I would hope that Parliament is not being asked to change this legislation simply because members of a Board, members appointed by the Government I may add, cannot agree on the cause of an aviation occurrence. As stated earlier, there is nothing in the legislation that which that decisions must be unanimous. I would think it would be suspicious and in fact highly improbable for all boards constituted by legislation to
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
arrive at unanimous decisions. Perhaps such boards that do are the ones that we should be looking into.
If there is dissension on this Board as the chairman has stated, then when and if this legislation receives Royal Assent, when selecting the five-member body to replace the present Canadian Aviation Safety Board, the Board should forgo the usual affiliation appointment process. I would urge the appointment of only the most qualified people to ensure that the Bill we are considering today will be operative and functional.
To be more pragmatic, if the only reason for the legislation is that the Board is divided, there are quicker and more effective ways to deal with this problem than to change the legislation in its entirety. The article to which I referred earlier states that the federally appointed members are deeply divided on what constitutes their duties and their responsibilities. The present act is clear in its definition under the power-granting section with respect to the duties of the Board, the duties of its chairperson and the duties of its investigators. If there is a dispute as to the interpretation of the meaning of sections of the current legislation, that dispute can certainly be settled by an application to the Federal Court for clarification of the duties imposed by the statute on the chairperson, the Board and even the investigators. I find it extremely difficult to reconcile my thinking to that of the chairperson who states that the only solution to this problem is a fast review and quick implementation of Bill C-2.
Certainly, the solution to making legislation operative is in its application by various boards appointed for that express purpose. Boards that are appointed for that purpose cannot keep running to the House to change legislation because, in their judgment, the legislation that they are entrusted to operate is inoperative. Members of those boards must use other means. There are other dispute-resolution mechanisms within our society.
After legislation is passed and becomes operative, as time goes on it may require minor changes or fine tuning, or as social conditions and circumstances change, the legislation may require some changes. Those changes can be accomplished by a variety of means. Changes to legislation can be made by making amendments to the statute or by making further regulations for which all statutes provide in order that the legislation becomes more effective. The legislation can be changed by the practice of the boards, or in the most dire of

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
circumstances, we may have to consider changing the appointments to those boards.
As I stated earlier, members of those boards cannot keep running to Parliament to cancel one Act over another. Acts cannot be replaced with another because of the reasons stated, simply those reasons for the change in this legislation.
The article about the annual report states: "Only expedient passage of similar legislation will resolve this issue considering the depth of division". Can one imagine the floodgates of legislation that would be before the House if every administrative board was allowed to come before the House when it found itself in conflict or divided on an issue on which all board members could not agree?
The fundamental purpose of government agencies and boards is to follow the statutory powers given to them by the legislation, and to perform their duties within the framework of providing natural justice to those who are directly affected by the legislation. The tenets of natural justice do not only apply to those people who are directly affected by the legislation which is being discussed. The tenets of natural justice also apply to the manner in which board members come to their decision and follow the decision-making process.
Decision-makers are obligated to give reasons for their decisions. After hearing all the evidence, if a decision-maker cannot in good conscience agree with his or her colleagues, he or she is bound by the oath taken not to vote accordingly just for the sake of unanimity. The decision-maker must vote by his or her conscience on the strength and the weight of the evidence which has been accepted. It would be most imprudent for the House to consider this legislation if the only reason for its passage is the division of the Board. The floodgates would open and perhaps never close.
Another perceived difficulty with the present legislation is the Director of Investigations' exclusive authority to conduct probes and report to the Board. Some members on the Board interpret this section to mean that they have a responsibility to satisfy themselves about the work performance of the staff. Other members on the Board should feel that they have a right to actively
participate in the day-to-day operations of the Board, including visiting the accident sites.
The sections in the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act give the Board power to hire employees necessary to conduct the work of the Board. That includes the person referred to in Section 9 who is the Director of Investigations who has exclusive authority to direct the conduct of investigations. With respect, this is the only problem with the present legislation. It is not sufficient reason to request the passage of new legislation. It would be my hope that the purpose for introducing new legislation would be more substantive than the reason we have heard, that the Board is divisive. I invite our friends to inform us of the main reasons and purpose for the new legislation referred to as Bill C-2.
Perhaps one of the reasons for this new legislation is the multimodal requirement for an accident board to investigate all forms of transportation occurrences, not only aviation. I will return to that question later in my submission.
When one looks at the size of Canada and its climate, there are very few problems not affected by geography or climate, or both. In a country as large as Canada, transportation is more than the provision of services for travel by air, land or sea. A country like ours must develop a philosophy and a concept that meets the needs and expectations of all Canadians to develop a transportation system that is economical, efficient, and above all safe.
What is the intent of Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Transportation Accident Investigation Board? As the title states, the intent is to investigate accidents and occurrences that happen on land, sea, air, or on the pipelines.
I am advised that the fundamental function of the Board is to prevent transportation accidents or occurrences, and to investigate the reasons for accidents or occurrences. From the title of the Bill, it is submitted that not enough impetus is given to the fact that there is a dual role, one of prevention and one of investigation. Therefore, the name of the Bill should be changed to better reflect the purpose and the intent of the legislation.
We have also been advised that the intent of the legislation is to create a strong, independent board. In my understanding, an independent board means that it has no allegiance to any Ministry, group, or to any external body. Of necessity, an independent board must
April 17, 1989

make a total break with all forms of Government. It must be completely independent, and its only responsibility is to the Canadian people in dealing with those major issues of safety.
We all agree with the concept and the intention of independence. However, we cannot say one thing and do another. Bill C-2 states that a five-member board is to be established, or not more than a five-member board is to be established. That language is not precise and the Bill should be more specific as to the number of members who should sit on the board.
The Bill also states that a chairperson is to be selected from the five-member board. However, he or she is not elected by the other members of the board. He or she will be appointed by the Minister of Transport. If something happens to the chairperson the Minister appoints a successor, independent of any advice from the board.
As a preliminary observation, we would suggest that the Minister appoint the five-member board and let the board elect its own chairperson. The board will set out by regulation the term of office and the other vital functions that it feels the chairperson should accomplish while he or she sits as chairperson of that board.
Bill C-2 states what the duties of the chairperson should be. The chief executive officer of the board has exclusive responsibility for all personnel matters, all financial matters, all property matters, all internal management of the board, directing staff and the work of the staff, directing and apportioning the work of the staff, and directing and apportioning the work of the board members.
It has always been my understanding that all board members are equal and the chairperson is only the first among equals. Perhaps this is the most fundamental problem with the previous legislation and the proposed legislation before us.

Mr. Speaker, last week, in honour of Citizenship Week, I attended a citizenship court at Vancouver Technical School where 65 new Canadians from 28 countries were sworn in as citizens.
Judge Angela Kan spoke eloquently on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship. Mr. Speaker, today is Equality Day, the fourth anniversary of the coming into effect of Section 15 of the Charter.
Equality Day reminds us of the important principles enshrined in our Constitution which guarantee all individuals equal access to the protection and benefits of the law without discrimination.
A measure of the fairness of our society is provided by the existence of these equality rights. A far more telling measure, however, is the extent of their application. Canadian women are acutely aware of the gap that still exists between equality in principle and equality in practice.
Since September 1984, our Government has worked with women to broaden their access to the kinds of opportunities essential to equality. Employment equity,
the Federal Contractors Program, our efforts to open up training opportunities to women, our pension reforms and our recently announced intention to broaden and equalize maternity and parental benefits are proof positive of our Government's commitment to make equality real for Canadian women.

Mr. Speaker, I follow up on what I said in this House on December 23. Tobacco farmers in Haldimand-Norfolk and throughout Canada are seeing major restructuring go on through and in their industry due to the Government's policies. During the election the Government committed itself to a $30 million program for Redux to support these farmers.
To date, these farmers have not seen a penny from this program. I urge the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski) to obtain approval from Treasury Board for this program quickly and to assure producers that once applications are completed the cheques will be in the mail immediately.

sary as Law Day. This year's "access to justice" theme is one that I strongly endorse. It reflects the right of every Canadian to have equal access to information about the laws and the legal institutions of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was implemented four years ago today. That particular section guarantees each and every individual's right to equal protection and equal benefit under the law without discrimination. Because of that legal instrument, all Canadians, men and women alike, have access to a greater freedom and a vast number of opportunities.

Equality Day holds special significance for Canadian women who were among the most active and effective proponents of entrenching equality rights in our Constitution.

While we should not rest on our laurels, we can see that the House has a record number of female Members of Parliament, six of whom sit on the Cabinet. Today, women can be found in every field, every profession, every walk of life. I am proud to be part of a Government that actively supports women in their quest for equality in all walks of life.

Mr. Speaker, today Canadian women are celebrating the anniversary of Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms coming into force. This clause guarantees equality to the women of Canada.
Canadian women depend on the women's Legal Education and Action Fund to use the Charter to promote women's equality. We also need equal access to education and jobs, child care and pay equity. For those programs we need a Government truly committed to women's rights.
How is the Conservative Government celebrating this anniversary? It is funding a gathering of REAL Women, a group opposed to the inclusion of women's rights in the Charter and dedicated to turning back the clock. This action shows us what the Government really thinks of the Constitution and of women's equality.

only been a band-aid approach to the real problem fanners face.

Mr. Speaker, despite our government's many initiatives over the past few years to improve our environment, a SORE-COM poll published yesterday shows that less than a third of the people in Quebec believe their governments' contention that say they give as much importance to the environment as to economic growth.
For 92 percent of Quebecers, the environment should get the same priority as the economy. Quebecers are most concerned about acid rain and air pollution.
The people of Quebec want effective clean-up programs and tough laws with drastic penalties for polluters.

subtopic: SPONSORING OF WORLD SUMMIT BY CANADA URGED
SPONSORING OF WORLD SUMMIT BY CANADA URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Nations Children's Fund is anxiously waiting for the Canadian Government to sponsor a special conference on the dark future of the world's children.
Through the development of low-cost health measures such as immunization and oral rehydration therapy, the annual death of children has dropped from 25 million in 1950 to 14 million in 1988. However, the debt burden has forced Third World Governments to cut health budgets by 50 per cent. It is the children who will pay the price. For lack of a 50 cent vaccine, millions of children will die. Without rehydration therapy another 2.5 million will die.
The Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) fully endorsed the Prime Minister's statement that alleviating poverty must be given a new priority on national and international agendas.
I urge the Government to live up to its commitment to help the world's poorest countries and people by sponsoring a summit for children where developing and developed nations can address the problems of the world's children living in poverty, including those in Canada. Canada could help save millions of children by sponsoring a world summit.

Mr. Speaker, in Canadian homes across this land these days there is no joy. There is no laughter. There are no light hearts. Rather, the lights bum late into the night for stretched out on the kitchen tables of the country the new 62-page simplified income tax guide plagues, torments and mystifies the average Canadian.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised Canadians that his new tax reform would make the tax system simpler for all. But it is not simple, it is much more difficult.
In the last reported tax year over one-quarter of Canadians made mistakes in filling out their tax returns. That was before tax reform.
Accountants and tax professionals are thanking the Finance Minister for the favour. Their business is booming. Now not only do Canadians have to pay taxes, they have to pay to pay taxes.
We are calling for the Government to keep its promise. What we have seen in this year's tax form is yet another broken promise by a Government that has a long track record of broken promises.
I call on the Minister to undertake immediately to devise a truly simplified form. I suggest that those ordinary Canadians who are now carrying the largest tax burden be consulted during this process.

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to draw to the attention of the House the fact that today is Equality Day. It is an occasion to celebrate the equality rights of all residents of Canada. In particular it gives us the opportunity to review the progress made in a practical sense by the women of Canada.
April 17, 1989

Canadian women played an important part in securing the equality rights for all of us here today. Women now represent 43 per cent of Canada's labour force. They comprise almost one-quarter of our country's business owners.

speechtext: When the House recessed for lunch, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi) had the floor. There were four minutes left for his intervention.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Any questions or comments? Debate.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to speak in support of Bill C-2, an Act to establish a Transportation Accident Investigation Board.
This Government recognizes that a thorough and objective accident investigation is crucial to transportation safety. From such studies we learn, document, and implement improved procedures and endeavour to find better and safer materials and technologies.
Transportation has played a crucial role in the development of this nation. Canadians have come to depend on,

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
and expect, safe and efficient modes of transportation. Our record has been enviable. However, we cannot rest on our laurels. We must remain ever vigilant, incorporating new technologies and procedures where applicable and establishing appropriate institutions as required.
Our Government has endeavoured to improve transportation safety at every opportunity. The revision of the Aeronautics Act in 1985, the upgrading of the safety amendments to the Canada Shipping Act in 1987 and the Railway Safety Act in 1988 are a testament to this fact. In keeping with this determination, the proposed TAIB legislation will create a new, independent board entrusted with the authority to investigate and report on accidents involving the marine, rail, and commodity pipeline modes of transportation as well as that of air mode. This multi-modal board proposal was developed in response to the evident need to separate accident investigation from the safety regulation function in all of these vital modes of transportation in Canada.
In drafting the TAIB Bill we have had the benefit of experience since 1984 with the CASB Act and we have learned a great deal from that experience, including the difficulties which have led to so much recent concern.
As well, following circulation in June, 1987, of some preliminary suggestions and the tabling last July of former Bill C-142 we have had the benefit of advice from many sources. We received valued comments from all elements of the transportation industry as well as from organizations as the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Maritime Law Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
The Deschenes study on maritime casualty investigations has been very helpful, as has the Hickling evaluation of the CASB. Comments from the Hon. Mr. Justice John Sopinka, before his appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada, have also been of great assistance.
Serious consideration was given in the determination of the structure and composition of the new board. The creation of one multi-modal board offers distinct advantages which other formats do not provide.
It affords consistency in the application of standards while, at the same time, respecting the unique requirements of the individual modes. The multi-modal format will ensure consistency of treatment for those involved in transportation accidents in all modes. Each mode can
learn from the experience of the others, and much scientific, medical and other expertise can be applied across all modes.
To ensure that the respective differences between modes are considered the Bill provides in Clause 10 that three separate directors of investigation will be designated; one each for air and marine investigations, and one for rail-commodity pipeline investigations.
While ensuring recognition of the uniqueness of each transportation mode's needs, the Bill also provides that in appointing members to the new board the Governor in Council must appoint those who, and I quote:
-will ensure that the members are, collectively, knowledgeable about air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline transportation.
With these measures, I believe we can be confident that appropriate attention will be directed to accident investigation in each transportation mode as required, and yet we can rest assured that no one mode will be afforded a disproportionate degree of resources.
The new board will be independent. It will have jurisdiction to investigate a wide range of accidents, incidents, conditions and situations, and be mandated to report publicly on all findings as to the contributing factors and causes of accidents. Most important, the new board will be required to make recommendations to avoid repetition of similar accidents in the future.
The issue of board structure and composition was given very serious consideration. Independent advice was sought as to the most effective and efficient composition of the new board.
The TAIB Bill precisely clarifies the respective roles and responsibilities of the board members, the chairman, the directors of investigation and the board staff.
The chairman will be the chief executive officer of the board and will supervise and direct the work of the board and the staff. The board chairman will have the responsibility for the internal management of the board, including personnel, financial and property matters.
As with any other deputy head of a federal agency, the duties of the chairman will also include such responsibilities as directing and apportioning the work of the members and staff, calling and chairing board meetings, approving budgets and so forth.
April 17, 1989

The present Bill is drafted to give board members, acting as a unit, full responsibility for establishing the board's policies in key areas. The board members will be fully responsible for board activities. This responsibility will include the establishment of general policies to be applied when determining the causes of accidents, when finalizing board reports on those accidents and when making recommendations to improve safety.
It is intended that the board members shall apply their background and expertise not to conducting investigations for which very competent staff will be employed, but to weighing the contributing factors identified by the investigators.
The board as a whole will have the over-all responsibility for accident investigation, for making findings as to the contributing factors and causes of these accidents, and for issuing reports which contain recommendations based on their findings.
The board as a whole will determine which accidents are to be investigated while the directors of investigation will be responsible for directing the content of those investigations.
The board as a whole will review the reports of the accident investigators, obtain information from them as board members may see fit and, ultimately, determine the final board findings as to the causes and contributing factors, and approve final board reports.
Most important, board members are to make appropriate recommendations based on their findings and designed to prevent repetition of similar accidents.
As I noted earlier, board members set policies, by-laws and regulations for conducting the board's business. The Bill makes clear that the chairman must act in accordance with these policies, by-laws and regulations.
To carry out the actual investigation of accidents the Bill specifically establishes three positions for directors of accident investigation. These persons will be charged with directing the conduct of accident investigations on behalf of the board. They will have exclusive authority to carry out this function. However, they will exercise their authority in accordance with the policies established by the Board. Investigative staff will report to them. Their reports will be reviewed by the board members. The directors of investigation will then be required to con-
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
duct such further investigations as the Board may request.
The Board will be entitled to adopt and issue the investigators' report as its official report, or the Board may disagree with it in whole or in part and issue a final board report independent of the investigators' findings. The investigators' report would remain on record as submitted to the Board and be part of the record that may be accessed by the public.
The delineation of responsibilities between the board members and the investigators is obvious and deliberate. It is the duty of board members to review the reports of investigators and then make their determinations on the basis of this material and any other relevant information that they may have. Consequently, it is essential that the board members be able to review the reports of the investigators objectively.
With the deliberate provision of this separation of duties, board members will be free to disagree if they wish with investigators' reports, and there will be no question that the board members have been unduly influenced by investigative staff, or vice versa. This arrangement will enable board members to conduct their review and make their findings objectively. Parties with a direct interest who then make representations to the Board on review of circulated draft reports, or at public inquiries, can thus be confident that their representations are given equal weight by board members along with the reports prepared by the investigators.
Establishment of an independent board to investigate accidents for the rail and marine sectors, as well as the air mode, is clearly desirable. The TAIB will be completely independent and separate from any Department of Government. It will be handed a clear and precise mandate to investigate accidents and practices in each of the critical transportation modes in Canada.
The clearer definition of the roles of the board members, chairman and directors of investigation in the proposed TAIB Act should enable the new board to function effectively, efficiently and expeditiously.
The Board shall act as an impartial arbiter. It will not seek to lay blame or liability. Its sole purpose is to determine cause and to recommend changes to ensure future safety. It will judiciously investigate accidents in an open and public fashion. Interested parties will be welcome at investigations and will be in receipt of the Board's draft reports.

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Quality accident investigation is essential to ensure improved transportation safety. The new board will improve the quality of accident investigations in rail, marine, as well as air. This will lead to even better safety recommendations to help us avoid similar accidents in the future.
We all want to be confident that investigations are conducted fairly and objectively. The total independence of the new board will provide this objectivity. The investigators in the rail and marine modes will no longer be linked to the safety regulators. Potential conflicts of interest will be eliminated.
The Canadian transportation community at large strongly supports the creation of an independent transportation accident investigation board for all modes.
I truly believe that all Members support the basic objective of the Bill, that is, to improve the quality of accident investigation policies and procedures so that our transportation system can be made even safer for the future.
I hope that the Bill will be considered quickly so that this objective can be realized as soon as possible.
I look forward, along with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to working with the Standing Committee on Transport to ensure that, in all respects, this Bill will achieve its objective to the fullest extent possible. If that means considering some modifications to the provisions of the Bill, we are prepared to do so.
As a Government we will not compromise public safety for expediency. TAIB is not a stop-gap measure or an interim solution. Rather, it is a product of the Canadian Government's constant effort to improve safety in all modes of transportation. The new Transportation Accident Investigation Board embodies lessons we have learned, and attempts to anticipate foreseeable needs.
As a responsible Government we have observed, listened and now we have tabled this legislation. I trust that all Members of the House will respond in kind with equal appreciation for the need for swift passage of this critical Bill.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park.

Madam Speaker, I was pleased to hear that the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) welcomed the contributions and recommendations of John
Sopinka and the Canadian Bar Association, two outstanding authorities in this area and especially outstanding in terms of drafting Bills. The recommendations that both John Sopinka and the Canadian Bar Association made to the Government were that this Bill does not provide the Board the independence that it needs, that there is too much control and too much power given to the chairman and directors of investigation. Since the Minister of State for Transport stated in the House that the Government found the recommendations of the Canadian Bar Association and John Sopinka very helpful, can she tell us why her Government did not implement the main recommendations of these two bodies?

As I also mentioned, during the consultation we heard from the Hon. Justice Sopinka, from the Bar Association and from other groups and interested parties as far as the safety Acts were concerned. We took into consideration all the input we received, not just the two that the Hon. Member mentions. Certainly as that Bill comes before the standing committee, there are opportunities for making recommendations and making suggestions. We do feel in the drafting that we have taken into consideration all input, partly from the Bar, partly from Justice Sopinka, and also from the other groups as well. Madam Speaker, the Minister has made much about the independence of the Board. She mentioned something about the findings being made public and available, et cetera. April 17, 1989

24.2-must be allowed for the Minister to respond before it is publicly released.

Madam Speaker, my question through you to the Minister of State for Transport is: In my presentation earlier today I talked about the potential role for the Transport committee in actually being given the freedom to fully examine this legislation, the freedom to consult whoever the committee deems appropriate, whether they be in this country or the United States or elsewhere. Transportation Accident Investigation Board
duration of its hearings and all the matters that it deems appropriate?

I look forward to that co-operation in committee to make sure that we can move this quickly. As the Hon. Member knows, the chairman of a committee is the individual who is responsible, along with the steering committee if he forms such, to decide what action the committee will take, who they will hear and what time frames they will work under. Madam Speaker, three very short questions to the Minister of State. I was interested in her remarks about the records that will be accessible by the public. My question is: How soon will they be accessible to the public, when and where?
The second question is with respect to the multimodal concept and her comments that they should ensure consistency. My question is: Consistency in what area?
The third question is also to the Minister and is with regard to the duties of the chairperson and chief executive officer. Does she not feel that those duties are so onerous that that position should be split into two separate categories?

Madam Speaker, if I could start with the last question first. As far as it being a very large task for the chairperson and chief executive officer that is going to depend on the individual who is in the chair and his or her abilities to function there. As to the consistency in all modes, by having one investigative body or one board looking at all investigations, we can make sure that there is consistency in application of investigation methods in the assessing of the material. The information that comes through will be done by one board in all modes. They will be able to share from each other's responsibilities and each other's expertise in making those decisions. We feel over all that

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
it will make for a more knowledgeable board by sharing of expertise.
As to the first question about records and how soon they will be available to the public, I am sorry, I don't understand what the Hon. Member is referring to. I would like further explanation on that, if I may, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I thought that the Minister had said in her remarks that all the transcripts or the records would be made available to the public. Did I not hear that properly? I am wondering if I heard that properly.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, I have the feeling I have been here before on the same subject several times since 1968. While some of my colleagues on all sides might think that I have been here too long, I want them to know that I do not think so.
Hear, hear!

Until I do think so, I am going to stay, the Lord willing.
I have heard much about the independence of accident investigation boards, whether it be airline investigations, railway accidents, pipelines, or marine accidents. There has always been a question about their so-called independence.
Too often the boards were run by those who formulated the laws and regulations and were charged with the responsibility of enforcing them. They were also the judge and jury, and not too often convicted themselves.
We hear much about the independence of this board. Frankly, I believe it should be able to present its report and make it public the day it is ready, press conference
and all. If there is anything fundamentally bad or perceived to be bad about it, those concerned can appeal. If that does not work, they can go to the Federal Court, just like any other citizen of this country. I see no reason why the Minister should get an advance copy of the report.
While I have not yet read the whole Bill, clause by clause, I have found nothing that says anyone else concerned can get a confidential copy of the report in advance. I suggest that provision of an advance copy to the Minister weakens the independence of the Accident Investigation Board.
While some may disagree with me, particularly those in the trucking industry, I think the legislation should also cover trans-boundary, international and interprovincial trucking. One day a semi-transport with a couple of pup trailers will plow into the ground floor of an apartment block and everyone will ask what happened. It is inevitable.
With Bill C-19 we were promised that there would be a uniform set of regulations to which all the provinces would agree. The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) will recall the committee dealing with Bill C-19 when the Canadian Truckers Association begged the Government not to bring that legislation into place until everything else was in place first and there was agreement with the other jurisdictions in the 10 provinces and two territories on a uniform set of regulations, rules and conditions under which interprovincial transboundary trucking could operate. We still do not have such agreement. It is a jungle out there.
I understand that my own province refuses to even discuss the subject with the federal authority. According to the Constitution of Canada, going back to the BNA Act, the national government had jurisdiction under international and trans-border trucking until the early 1950s, when it gave it up to let the provinces administer it. Since then we have seen them run off in 10 different directions, and it still continues in spite of what the Government told us.
A Transportation Accident Investigation Board that will cover air, rail, marine and pipeline will have to be a large operation. Someone who is an ideal investigator of an aircraft will not be very good with pipelines, and vice-versa. You cannot hire these kinds of people at the Canada Employment Centre, or off the street. They
April 17, 1989

have to be experts. It will have to be a large operation, which I support, but there must be a commitment to it by the Government. There had better be a lot of money provided for this in the Budget to make sure there is the capacity to appoint and hire the best possible people for the board.
I do not want a repeat of the past. I remember a famous incident when an alderperson from Edmonton was put on the Board of Directors of Air Canada. When asked about her qualifications she said that she had flown a few times. We certainly do not want someone on an investigation board who is not knowledgeable about the industry. The people appointed to these boards should be experienced and competent.
There have been five Ministers of Transport since 1980, and almost as many Ministers of State for Transport. Jean-Luc Pepin opposed deregulation and that was the end of him. It was the Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Axworthy) who started all this nonsense of the nirvana of the marketplace, private enterprise and deregulation. In spite of the warnings from the experts outside Parliament, that government proceeded with deregulation in 1982, before there were any laws or regulations. The Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and now the Member for Roberval (Mr. Bouchard) were the succeeding Ministers. All five of them told us repeatedly in the committee that there would be no compromise on safety, security, inspection, enforcement and investigation.
This time we will not take those assurances at face value. If we cannot take the Government's word, it had better state in the Budget how much money it will provide, how many people it will involve, and what kind of people. If it is in the Budget, we might believe it.
We were accused of trying to frighten the public. Every Minister since the beginning of deregulation was repeatedly warned about the inadequacies of the system. These warnings were not just from Members of Parliament; they were from expert witnesses who knew what they were talking about. There were scores of hearings, including hearings on cabooses, hearings on the Freedom to Move White Paper, the National Transportation
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Act and the Trucking Act. There were hundreds of witnesses and on these and other occasions it was pointed out that safety and security inspection and enforcement was insufficient. Yet there was a lack of follow-up action.
I would like to remind Hon. Members of one witness in particular. One sure as heck could not call him a raving socialist. He was the immediate past head of the American Federal Aviation Administration, a Reagan appointee. He appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and not only urged us but pleaded with us not to deregulate until we had everything else in place in all modes of transportation. He admitted very plainly and honestly what had happened in the United States and told us not to make the mistakes they had made, but to learn the lessons of the American experience. I could not find a Minister and I could not even find a small majority of the Transport Committee who would agree with the man.
This man told us to have in place, before deregulating, enough controllers, enough inspectors, enough enforcement, enough runway capacity, enough terminal capacity and enough passenger and baggage security capacity. He told us to have that in place first and then to deregulate. The truckers told us the same thing.
Representatives of the Canadian Air Transport Association, Canadian owners and pilots, air traffic controllers and the machinists' union appeared before the committee and most of them said they were in favour of deregulation but did not think we were ready. Boy, were they right.
We were told ad nauseam that there would be no compromise on safety. But what do we continue to get under the last four Ministers of Transport? There have been cut-backs, reductions and restraint. This is after they have told us that there would be no compromise. That is why we will not accept the Minister's word or the Government's word this time. It had better be in writing, on paper and irrevocable.
If the Treasury Board or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) refuses to grant the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs.

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Martin) the kind of wherewithal that is required, then I think those Ministers should ask why and resign to the applause of the entire nation.
No matter what one thinks of the deficit or the national debt, in the last four years Ministers of Transport have done nothing but play fast and loose with the well-being of the travelling public in the name of restraint, cut-backs and the deficit, and with the safety and security of the facilities for the workers in the transportation industry. From what I have seen in some sectors of the transportation industry, I am amazed that the industry has done as well as it has with the tools given to it to do the job.
I do not see how we can have an effective accident investigation board without that kind of sign-on-the-dotted-line commitment. I do not want to have to go through this again. I have been through too many hearings, too many debates, too many pieces of legislation and way too many Ministers who never did follow through and do the job. In my experience so far with this Minister, the same thing applies. He is a nice fellow. There is nothing personal about it. It ain't his cup of tea. It is not what you could call his long suit, and I am not talking about his underwear!
We have to try to put the round pegs into the round holes and the square pegs into the square holes. In the transportation industry in Canada since the late 1970s, the opposite has been the case. This time, I hope the Government will put its action where its mouth is. We have heard all of this before ad nauseam.
I remember the days of Otto Lang, the late unlamented. It was very interesting this morning to listen to my good friend from New Brunswick who led off for the Official Opposition. I was hoping he would have the courtesy to blush. He was chairman of the Transport Committee when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Axworthy) brought in deregulation. Butter would not melt in the mouths of the Liberal members of the Transport Committee. They were telling us how good this was, but the Tories kicked the heck out of them. Then the Liberals got defeated and the Tories came in. I'll be darned. For the first year of the new Parliament, back in 1984, I sat here listening to Liberals making Conservative speeches and Conservatives making Liberal speeches. I must confess I got a little confused.
The Government is really not committed to treating transportation as a public utility. It is not prepared to treat it as something that must be regulated. We must make the transporters perform. I have no objection to
the transporters getting a reasonable return on their investment, but we cannot leave it to them. We cannot have airlines in charge of the inspection of passengers and luggage at airports. That has to be done by the Department of Transport. We cannot have the railways inspecting their own equipment with their shortage of car inspectors.
The Government has allowed the owners and operators of the transportation industry to have their way. As long as they can make a buck, they are called successful. This Government or another one like it, God forbid, will kill more people because this Minister and the previous three Ministers as well as the previous Government have in fact compromised on safety, security, inspection and enforcement. Unless the Government comes up in the Budget with all the wherewithal to do it right, we will not believe it and we will fight it to make it do so.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the speech by the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party, and I remember that a few years ago when an accident happened in Gander and also recently with the accident in Dryden, all the Opposition Parties screamed bloody murder and asked for a royal commission of inquiry. Today, we have introduced a Bill that will separate investigators from the people who enforce the legislation, and they don't like that. My first question is: I would like to know what they don't like about a system which, once and for all, will separate investigators from those who enforce the regulations. My second question is, whether they have an alternative policy. If they do, I wish they would let us know because they keep criticizing the Government but never suggest any concrete alternatives. My last question is this: If a socialist party ever came to power, what amounts would it appropriate in this area?

Madam Speaker, I apologize to my colleague. I missed his first couple of sentences. He said something about Gander, which I do not pretend to know anything about.
The hon. gentleman asks what we would do. As I said in my speech, and I meant it, we would ask the Government to treat transportation as a public utility. It is something that everyone in Canada has to use both directly and indirectly. It cannot be left up to the whims of the operators and owners of each mode of transportation, whether they are publicly or privately owned, to
April 17, 1989

operate what is first in their best interests, the bottom line. That cannot be allowed.
I forget the other question of my hon. friend, however, not once did I mention the words NDP in my entire speech. If my hon. friend would like me to give him a 40-minute exercise in NDP transportation policy, I would be delighted and willing to ask the House for unanimous consent for me to have another 40 minutes.

speechtext: The Hon. Minister of State for Transport.

I appreciate and thank the Minister for her attempts to reassure me. I recall when I was assured there were enough railway inspectors that it turned out there were 19 for 100,000 miles of track in Canada and over 150,000 units of rolling stock.
We were repeatedly assured there would be enough air traffic controllers. Does the fact that there is a backlog of more than 1,200 investigations not tell the Minister of State something? Does that not make the Minister and the foggy bottoms in the Department of Transport
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
realize and understand that they are not only away behind but they have to do more than catch up?
Of course, some people will be recruited from the Department of Transport and from the National Transportation Agency. I expect that expertise will have to be found in other countries and brought in. Those people are not hired down at the Canada Employment Centre. The Minister will have a sweet time getting this set up. I do not believe there are enough bodies in the Government. If all the Minister is going to do is hire ex-railway officers or airline officers, then the problem has not been solved.

4.(2) The Governor in Council shall appoint as members persons
who, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, are collectively
knowledgeable about air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline

I thank my colleague for that comment. However, I wish to suggest to her that we have had that before where, in the opinion of the Government, someone is qualified.
If my hon. colleague had been here for the number of years that I have, she would find out how that did not work. That is another reason the Standing Committee will now insist on sitting down with every appointee, and I do not care if it is in camera or not, to see whether or not the Standing Committee is prepared to recommend them. Too often the opinion of the Government is more designed to hand somebody a job than it is a matter of competence, background, and experience.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the speech of Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin). As transportation is one of his fortes that he has studied for a great many years, I would like to remind him that it sounded like we had deregulated safety. Nothing could

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
be further from the truth, and the Hon. Member knows that.
Compromised on it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Canada has a very good safety record. In fact, it is one of the top safety records world-wide in any mode the Hon. Member cares to choose. Certainly there are accidents, and that is what the Bill is all about. We are trying to prevent accidents. We want to ensure that we have the right means in place to prevent accidents.
The Bill addresses the need to improve on safety and to ensure that it has been properly studied. The Government did bring forward the Aeronautics Act amendments in 1985, of which the Hon. Member was a part and studied that legislation. There were also the Canada Shipping Act amendments in 1987, and the railway shipping Act of last year. The Hon. Member was also a part of those.
The Hon. Member talked about interprovincial trucking. Highways are a provincial matter. Each province has its own police force which works within its own province. It makes no difference whether the truck is going from one province to the next. Why should it not be maintained and the safety part adjudicated from within each individual province? Why should we attempt to put this into an intermodal scheme of things when it is already under the jurisdiction of each individual province?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: A short rebuttal from the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden.

Thank you for your patience, Madam Speaker, with all of us. In my opinion, in some respects safety was deregulated when the exit and entry regulations for airlines and charter aircraft were cancelled. It was left wide open. As long as someone could get a bank loan, lease a couple of airplanes, and hire a laid-off crew at half the wages, he was in business. There may have been no mechanics or hangar, but he was in business. How many dozens have started up? It is even worse south of the border. It seems to me that that is deregulating safety.
The same thing has applied in other sectors of the transportation industry. They are fundamental to the national economy, and whether they are privately or publicly owned, by their very nature they are natural monopolies. Therefore, they have to be regulated and controlled, particularly in the areas of safety, inspection,
security enforcement, and all the other things I have mentioned.
There are not only one or two items that crop up now and again. It is a large ball of wax, and so far all the Government has done is melt it.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) that Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Transportation Investigation Board and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to address the legislation before us, that is, the establishment of a new Transportation Accident Investigation Board.
I must begin my remarks by saying that the Minister's decision to model this new Transportation Accident Investigation Board after the CASB is on the right track.
April 17, 1989

However, I believe the Minister is putting the cart before the horse. Accident investigation is of primary importance to ensure high levels of safety standards. Many recommendations stemming from investigations have contributed to this country's high level of safety regulations which protect air travellers on a daily basis.
Why is this Government rushing the creation of this new board? Why will this Government not wait for the findings of the judicial inquiry into the Dryden crash? Why will it not wait to hear from Justice Estey's review of the circumstances surrounding the Gander crash?
The logic is that an inquiry always precedes legislation, similar to the previous process when the Dubin inquiry into air safety provided the building block for the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act. Or, is it that this Government is not interested in the findings and recommendations of the Estey review and the Dryden inquiry?
A recent Angus Reid poll indicates that Canadians think air travel in this country is less safe than it was, and an overwhelming majority wants this Government to show some leadership and do something about it. The poll also suggests that Canadians want firmer regulations of air travel. Air safety should be this Government's first priority. Let me tell the House why.
On Friday, March 10, I received word that Air Ontario's Flight 363 crashed in Dryden shortly after take-off. Some 24 people lost their lives and many more were injured. The victims' families want to know what happened. They want to be reassured that our airways are safe. They want to know that regulations have been followed.
In the days following the crash we heard of a three-year old Transport Canada report which pinpointed the Wawa to Kenora region as one of the most dangerous flying zones in the country. We also heard again in the same report that northern Ontario's accident rate is higher than the national average. This is frightening, and it is totally unacceptable.
It is unacceptable to the people of northern Ontario, and it should be a top priority of this Government. This is also why members of the Liberal Party believe that this legislation could have waited until all the facts are in.
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
This new Transportation Accident Investigation Board will not address the immediate issue of air safety in this country. It will not address the immediate issue of air safety inspectors, nor will it address the immediate issue of air traffic controllers and the perilous effects of deregulation.
Deregulation of Canada's air industry has created some major difficulties with respect to air safety in this country. This Government accelerated the legislative process of deregulation and this led to several key mistakes in the final legislation which have left air safety in peril. I know and I need not be reminded that deregulation was introduced by a Liberal Government. The Liberal Party supports the basic concept of deregulation, but it was totally opposed to the rapid process adopted by this Government. This Government's failure to include a key clause in the final legislation, which could have protected remote and distant communities such as those located in northern Ontario from loss of services as a result of deregulation, has contributed to today's problems with aviation safety.
Bill C-2 will not restore faith in air safety. Canadians want assurances that our airways are safe. They want regulations which will protect them, and rightly so. I can tell Hon. Members of the House that this Government's failure to include this key clause has led to a loss in service. It has led to inadequate weather reporting facilities in my riding and across the whole northern part of this province. It has led to higher air incidences, and it has led to the loss of lives. I encourage the Minister to fly into my riding on a Saturday and see for himself the level of service being provided to northerners.
When this Bill was originally introduced last July, the Minister said at the time and I quote: "The National Transportation Act places safety at the top of our list of objectives. The Government takes this commitment seriously".
What has happened to this commitment? Given the crash at Dryden, the inefficient numbers of air safety inspectors, and the lack of air traffic controllers in this country, I fail to see this Government's commitment to air safety. How will this piece of legislation reassure Canadians that air safety is a priority with this Government?
I would like to turn to the new Transportation Accident Investigation Board's mandate. This legislation was to establish this Board as a totally independent body. It must be of the highest standards employing Canada's top experts in the field of transportation safety. Failure to provide these basic principles will lead to another situa-

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
tion such as we have seen with the Gander crash investigation.
Members of my Party cannot emphasize strongly enough the importance of waiting for the results of the judicial inquiry into the Dryden crash and the judicial review of the Gander crash before rushing ahead with this legislation.
The Dubin inquiry on aviation safety formed the basis of the legislation creating the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act, 1984. It boils down to basic common sense and logic. Waiting for these results will provide the Government with the necessary recommendations to create an accident investigation agency which will promote safety in Canada to the maximum efficiency and to ensure that the day-to-day operations of this agency will proceed with the least possible opportunities for dissension to set in.
It is also my hope that this Government will be bound by this new Transportation Accident Investigations Board's recommendations, such was the case with the CASB. The only difference is that Bill C-2 should ensure that the recommendations to the Government are adhered to.
In March 1987, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board completed a study of aviation accidents in the Wawa-Ke-nora region. The conclusions of this study indicated that situations involving pilots operating under visual flight rules pushing on into bad weather appeared to be a factor in the higher accident rate in this region. Further, this was some indication that weather facilities in northern Ontario, particularly 24-hour weather observations sites were not sufficient to counteract the difficulties of weather forecasting. Based on these findings the board made two safety recommendations and recommended that the Department of Transport and the Department of the Environment expedite the installation of automatic weather observing and reporting facilities in the Wawa-Kenora region. It also recommended that the Department of Transport institute a promotional campaign to improve pilot awareness of the extra efforts needed to conduct their safety operations throughout that region. Neither of these recommendations were acted upon. Had the Government listened to the experts, the Dryden crash could have possibly been avoided.
In closing, I urge this Government to listen closely to the recommendations being made by Members on this side of the House. They are sound and valid recommendations. I urge this Government to wait for the findings of the Estey review on the Gander crash and the judicial enquiry of the Dryden crash before proceeding with this legislation.

Madam Speaker, I thank the new Member for his remarks. The biggest problem with this situation is that when we get back to the Bill we will see that nothing has been changed from the CASB. speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the debate today on second reading of the legislation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to create the Transportation Accident Investigation Board.
Before I start I want to pay credit to the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), who was our lead speaker for our Party this morning. He raised a number of important concerns. As well I mention the dean of transportation in the House from our side, the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), who brings us a great deal of knowledge and experience.
I have a few brief comments to make before I discuss the legislation before us. It deals perhaps in some ways with safety by rail but it is also a much broader issue that has been raised by many members in Question Period and in other Debates, namely, VIA Rail and its possible future expansion-unlikely as that may be considering the responses from the Minister of Transport. I am speaking particularly of VIA Rail service in northern British Columbia. I had an opportunity to ride from Prince George to Goat River and return Friday evening. I want to thank the crew of that train with whom I had a chance to talk about the service, as well as the passengers who expressed their opinions to me in terms of how important this service is.
I also wish to thank VIA officials in Montreal who gave notice of my trip and ensured that I had all of the proper paperwork in place to be on board that train. Perhaps safety was involved with this trip. I say that because I had the opportunity to go up to the head-end of the train. Frankly, some of the equipment that the Liberal Government before this Government put in place has forced the railway to run with old furnaces on rails. That is a safety hazard. According to the press release of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) the new Transportation Accident Investigation Board will investigate causes of accidents, make recommendations to correct safety deficiencies, prepare public reports on its findings and, where possible, suggest ways to prevent recurrences.
According to the press release what the legislation will do is combine three existing organizations. They are the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, the Marine Casualty Investigations Branch of Transport Canada and the Railway Pipelines Investigation Directorate of the National Transportation Agency. As the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) said this morning I suppose most Members wish that we would not have to have such boards to investigate accidents, especially when they have to pick up the pieces and to take a look at what are often tragic accidents that happen in transportation in Canada. Of course we have to have a body to review such accidents to ensure that we learn from them and to ensure that regulations and legislation in the future will be introduced by the Government so that these carriers will not incur damage.
I would like to give an example as to why this legislation is important. In doing so I will reflect on some of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin) about responsibility. Whose responsibility is it to ensure that these carriers operate properly and that we do not end up with major accidents?
My example concerns a situation in my riding which is in northern British Columbia. It was brought to my attention by representatives of Lodge 1415 of the Brotherhood of Railway Carmen of the United States and Canada. They have an interesting situation similar to many communities where there is an interchange between two railroads. In this case it is the British Colum-
April 17, 1989

bia Railway owned by the Province of British Columbia and Canadian National with which we are all familiar.
In this case under the authority of the National Transportation Agency CN used to be required to have its trainmen inspect the cars before they were sent off on a train. These people are certified under the National Transportation Agency. For those who are familiar with northern British Columbia and Prince George, these trains are made up in the B.C.R. yard which is just south of Prince George. CN sends a locomotive and cabooses over to the B.C.R. yard and then takes the train from there to Winnipeg. Because B.C.R. is a provincially regulated railway the need to have certified inspectors look at those cars is avoided.
The Brotherhood of Railway Carmen think that this is important. They have raised the matter on a number of occasions with the National Transportation Agency. I will be raising it on their behalf again. I have told them that this legislation will be before the House today and likely tomorrow. We felt it would be a good idea to raise this issue in order to point out the concerns that there are.
The carmen conducted a survey concerning one particular train, Train No. 358 which goes from Prince George to Winnipeg. They had their brothers and sisters in Winnipeg report to them on the condition of the train when it arrived, especially in terms of any particular problems that there were with it. In this way they built evidence with respect to the safety of the railroad, which is their paramount concern. If they are required to be certified to send trains out why is the National Transportation Agency allowing a train to travel from Prince George to Winnipeg without being inspected?
In the month from January 13, 1989, to February 12, 1989, a survey of Train 358 was conducted. Normally it has about 75 to 100 cars on it. This survey was conducted by the Brotherhood. The results are as follows. Some 44 cars were reported in bad order, 22 of them for wheels. I asked the members of the brotherhood which of these bad orders were of particular concern because of potential derailment. Wheels are the most important aspect of the train to be inspected. Nine cars were cited for defective loads such as shifting of loads, bands coming loose and what have you. Eight cars had defects in connection with their braking systems. One can understand the concern over a braking system not working.
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Five cars had various defects concerning draft gears and couplers.
The people who conducted this survey feel that these 44 cars in one month on one train in the state in which they were in is unacceptable considering that these cars are travelling half way across the country in bad order status. However, we are at a point at which the Government and its regulatory agencies have allowed the carriers to govern themselves, to find ways to avoid just such situations as the one I have cited. What we have to be cognizant of when we are discussing the legislation that we are discussing today is what we have to face in the future.
It states in the Minister's release: "-and where possible suggest ways to prevent recurrences". In the case which I have cited I hope and trust that that will not occur after an accident has happened. I certainly intend to pass this information on to the Minister. A situation such as this should be investigated. There should be a report so that those people who are servicing the trains know and feel confident that they are safe and that all the communities along the line from Prince George to Winnipeg can be assured of rail safety.
If there are Members in the House who have concerns in other locations of the country then it is our duty to bring them to the attention of the Minister at the earliest possible opportunity.
I have one other situation which I would like to raise with Members in order to give them an appreciation of just what we are facing in terms of rail safety. I have more information from the same Brotherhood of Railway Carmen. They have particular duties to inspect trains to ensure that they are safe. In the particular case which I would like to cite now a worker alleges that there is a problem in identifying roller bearing noise when a train is going through inspection. I have spoken with the worker and he is prepared to provide additional information to investigators. In this case the worker alleges that the crew that was inspecting the train suggested that there was a problem with these roller bearings, that it was not identified by supervisory personnel and that the train or car went out. In this particular case we are talking about a north-east coal train with which people from western Canada are familiar. The train proceeded and in fact ended up derailing.
These employees of the railway feel that there is a concern about the safety of equipment and its reliability which may lead to derailments that we all hope will not happen. In this particular case it was on the British

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Columbia Railway again, a provincially regulated railway. It is of particular interest to us because the equipment is actually inspected by Canadian National Railway employees.
Let me get then to the legislation before us and before it goes to committee where there will be opportunity for people to air their views and, I hope, to call witnesses to look into this legislation. I hope there will be sufficient opportunity to research the area so that we end up with some good legislation.
One of the concerns we have is that while the legislation lays out in detail some of the membership requirements, as Hon. Members opposite have said, it is important that they be collectively knowledgeable about transportation issues. That is very important, Madam Speaker. But one of the issues I would like to raise is that there should be a section in the legislation, a direction to the Government to seek out all interested parties to see if they are interested in sitting on the board. I hope the Minister will attempt to include this.
One of the comments from my meeting on the weekend with the Railway Carmen is that nobody ever asks them. As the people who basically do that day-today work, through their organizations-perhaps a professional association or a union-they should have an opportunity to make comment and to sit in on the deliberations.
I would certainly encourage amendment to the legislation that gives direction to the Minister to seek some wide membership and to make sure all of the interested parties have an opportunity to participate in the discussion and the appointment of members.
I think a general concern of all Members should be that bodies such as the Transportation Accident Investigation Board be perceived as independent. I know it is often difficult for the Government to appear not to politically interfere. They have not had a particularly good record in that case. But in the future, I think boards like this that often have to review very tragic circumstances, should be above board and be given every opportunity to make comment. That is not going to necessarily be a part of the day-to-day goings on in this House, such as we see in Question Period, though ultimately it is this House's responsibility to deal with those issues. Let us keep it at arm's length. Let us keep it
professional, and offer an opportunity for all to have input.
Equal access should be given to all interested parties to the findings of any investigation. These interested parties should be clearly named by group, whether we are talking about a private company, union representatives, family members or accident victims. I think that is important.
I should say this Bill is long overdue because of the circumstances in our rail, air and water. I am not as familiar as many Members are about air transportation. However, having had to experience it in the last short while, I can certainly vouch that I have been commuting the hard way. It is not just the six hours to Prince George, B.C. It is sitting on those planes for what ended up last Friday to be a lot longer than that, spread over two days to get home. But we appreciate the work that the crews of these airlines and these railroads do to ensure that we, as travellers, can get home, not just Members of Parliament but Canadian travellers and our many visitors and to know that they are travelling in a safe and comfortable way.
The experience of the United States is a perfect example of some of the problems we may face in this country with deregulation. Undoubtedly, the additional airline traffic that we are seeing now at Pearson International Airport means that the Government and Transport Canada and boards like this will have to be ever vigilant to ensure that the proper regulations are followed and that when something does happen, this type of board is given the opportunity and the resources it needs to make a thorough investigation. I think our Transport critic from Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) made that point very clear. It is important that a body like this and the Government have the resources to carry out any of those necessary changes.
What is going to happen on Budget night? We do not know what the impact is going to be on this legislation. It may render this legislation useless. We hope that does not happen, but that could be the impact of the Budget of the Minister of Finance on April 27.
We hope that does not happen with a number of issues, be it in forestry or unemployment insurance or regional development. We do not want to see perhaps well-intentioned legislation, such as this, damaged by Government Members opposite voting it down by supporting a Budget that may gut the usefulness of this legislation and this board. I would like to hear assurances from the Minister that this will not happen and
April 17, 1989

that we will have the resources to ensure that proper investigations are carried out.
These kinds of boards are critical because they give that independence to the kinds of unfortunate accidents we have seen. I look forward to following the proceedings in the Transport Committee, although I am not a member of that committee. As you can see, Madam Speaker, from the representations made to me, the people who work in the transportation industry in my riding are concerned. It is opportunities like this and in correspondence with the Minister and department officials that we can raise the concerns of the people who work in the industry so that, hopefully, we will not need to have very many investigations under this board. I trust it will have a boring future and, if needed, the Government will give it the resources to be effective.
Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Transportation Accident Investigation Board
With respect to the financial conditions, I think resources have increased since 1984.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment.
I would like to go back to one of the Hon. Member's remarks he made earlier with respect to the independence of this Board, when he stressed the various problems involved in controlling the safety aspect and gave serveral examples.
It seems to me that the very purpose of the Bill before the House is to make the distinction in safety management between accident investigations and enforcement of safety regulations.
