I will rephrase my question: How can he claim that safety regulations can be followed and enforced today, if the whole purpose of the Bill is to separate the two aspects as much as possible?

Madam Speaker, I am not sure if I caught all of the Hon. Member's question but I will do my best to answer. First I will deal with having good people on the board to ensure that policies are followed. We should follow a practice that I hope is used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), that good, qualified people are appointed to these boards. They should be people who think independently and can be assured that when they are presented with advice and information from various departmental officials they can make an independent decisions about what they recommend. We hope that is what the Prime Minister does when he chooses members of his Cabinet. We trust that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) will do that when he considers appointees to this particular board. I hope he will be mindful of my comments about direction and ensuring a broad base of representation on the board. I hope he looks hard to find good people.
The Hon. Member asked how one applies the rules
and makes them work. That responsibility comes under the National Transportation Agency. I believe this body should review some of the authority that the National Transportation Agency has, just to see if the rules are carried out effectively on the ground.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in debate on Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Transportation Accident Investigation Board, and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof. Like the Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), I too have been here before. Except, unlike the Hon. Member, I had an opportunity to take a leave of absence for four years from the House and observe the work of the Government and the workings and process of the House from the outside. That was good experience. -
I was actually pleased when the Government was elected in 1984, because it promised it would consult grassroot Canadians.
We did.

They say they did. I had the good fortune of being Vice-President of the Canadian Polish Congress for two years. The Government swamped us with requests for input, requests for input on the multicultural Bill, on immigration matters, on transportation matters. What the Government does not realize is that these organizations do not have paid researchers and advisers. They do not have professional writers. Weeks and months were spent responding to the Government's request for input. What was done with that information? Nothing. It wasted Canadians' time.
The Government said it was consulting us and wanted our input, but what did it do with it? It paid no attention to us. If it implemented one suggestion from all these Canadians, then Canadians would say the Government is legitimate. It had all of that input, as it does from Justice Sopinka and the Canadian Bar Association on this Bill, but not one of their recommendations have been implemented. It makes the whole democratic process a farce and the Government should resign now. The first one who should resign is the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard).
April 17, 1989

In November, 1983,1 was the Parliamentary Secretary to the then Minister of Transport whose duty it was to monitor Bill C-163, an Act to establish the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, through all of the parliamentary stages. The Act came into effect in October, 1984. There was much debate at the time about whether the Government of the day should be implementing a unimodal transportation investigation agency or a multimodal board. The consensus of the day was that we should establish a unimodal agency. Of course, the logical travel mode to begin with was aviation, since Justice Dubin's Inquiry on aviation safety made this recommendation. He recommended separating safety regulations from accident investigation and establishing an independent investigating body.
The three Parties agreed that we should begin with a unimodal agency and, when such a board proved to function well, we would move to a multimodal investigating board as recommended by Bill C-2. When one looks at the previous legislation, Bill C-163 and Bill C-2, one sees that in most articles they are identical. Therefore, the Official Opposition agrees with the intent of Bill C-2, as stated in Article 7(1): "To advance transportation safety".
However, the fly in the ointment is that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board is not functioning well, as was demonstrated in the investigation of the Gander crash. To this day, three years after the crash, Canadians do not know the cause of the crash. Five members of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board concluded that it was caused by icing on the wings. Four members suspected that there may have been an explosion on board which had nothing to do with the icing theory.
The Conservative Government demonstrated that it cannot manage a unimodal board. How can it manage a multimodal agency? Why did the Government not call a judicial inquiry to answer the questions raised in the minority report of the four members? Transport Canada, in a leaked document, also did not agree with the icing theory. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) flip-flopped in his assessment of the findings on the cause of the Gander crash. With so many unanswered questions, why is the Government rushing this Bill through the House on an urgent basis?
The other week, all three Parties expressed condo-
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
lences to the families of the victims of the Dryden crash. Had the icing recommendations of the CASB reached the appropriate people, maybe condolences would not have had to be expressed in the House. I see nothing in Bill C-2 that would guarantee that the recommendations of the TAIB will be received by the principal players and implemented where and when necessary. The public and the Public Service working in Transport Canada have lost confidence in the Minister and in the Government.
Less than a month ago, we saw the headlines dealing with this issue. I do not have time to quote all of them, but I would like to share with Hon. Members this headline from The Ottawa Citizen which reads: "Senior bureaucrat resigns over air crash controversy". The article reads: "Another senior Transport official, said Lafrance, quit because he had lost the confidence of the Minister and the Deputy Minister. Lafrance also recently told the Minister that the Department had issued special wing icing warnings to all commercial airlines in January. He later admitted his Department had not sent the warning to Air Ontario until mid-March, five days after one of its planes crashed and killed 24 people at Dryden, Ontario".
Now the Minister has appointed Mr. Justice Willard Estey to review the record of the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Gander crash. The reference given to Mr. Justice Estey was that he could call witnesses who were not heard from before and could call for evidence in addition to going through the existing testimony. I was disappointed when I heard that Mr. Justice Estey will only review the evidence on hand. If he does that, naturally he will come to the same conclusion that the Minister wants; that is, he will support the icing theory.
There were witnesses to incidents just prior to the crash who were not called in to testify. As an example, a truck driver saw a ball of fire under the plane. Will that lead us to suspect that the crash was caused by icing on the wings, or was there an explosion? Why is Mr. Justice Estey not calling this truck driver to give evidence about what he observed?
What is the Government trying to cover up? Were unsafe explosives on board, was it sabotage? The mother of the killed pilot wants to testify before the inquiry of Mr. Justice Estey. Now she cannot. Why not?

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
How can the Government have the gall to bring in a multimodal transportation Bill when it cannot tidy up its act in one mode of travel? Look at what is happening at Pearson International Airport. People are losing confidence in air travel and in the Government. There is a shortage of air traffic controllers. There is a shortage of inspectors.
Why is there a shortage of air traffic controllers? Not long ago, during my time as Parliamentary Secretary, almost entire classes of air traffic controllers were being failed. Then there was some intervention and the same people re-wrote the exams and passed them. My own son wanted to be an air traffic controller. He wrote the exams and passed them. Six years later, he is still waiting to be called in for an oral interview. That is how the Government is running transportation in Canada.
We have a Government that cannot respond quickly to oil spills caused by marine accidents. We have a Government that is abandoning sections of VIA Rail routes. This is causing low morale, and we know what low morale does. Low morale will lead to more accidents. There appears to be no Government commitment to an adequate, safe transportation system.
Our Party is recommending that we wait for Mr. Justice Estey's findings and then bring in Bill C-2. By forcing the Bill through now, the Minister is putting the caboose before the engine, or does the Minister have a hidden agenda in this Bill? Is he trying to eliminate the four dissenters from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, four members who truly want to make air travel safer by obtaining the true cause of the Gander crash?
Looking at the expertise of the dissenting members, it is no wonder that Canadians and Americans are placing a great deal of importance on this minority report. Let us look at the qualifications of some of the members who submitted the minority report. Les Filotas has a Ph.D. in theoretical aeronautics. He is the most highly qualified Canadian in aeronautics. Captain Ross Stephenson is a Captain with Air Canada with over 30,000 hours of flying including 9,000 hours on the DC-8. If anyone would know whether to pursue the icing theory or the explosion theory, it would be Captain Ross Stephenson. Mr. Mussallem is an aeronautical engineer who also spent several years as a pilot with Wardair. With experts like that submitting a minority report, surely to goodness the Minister should have called a judicial inquiry right away. Now he wants to deal with a multimodal board. He should clean up his act in one mode first.
Let us look at Bill C-2. Clause 4 establishes a board to be known as the Transportation Accident Investigation Board consisting of not more than five full-time members appointed by Governor in Council. There are nine members investigating one mode and the Bill is recommending that a maximum of only five members shall explore all modes of travel. The Bill goes on to say that the Governor in Council shall appoint as members persons who, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, are collectively knowledgeable about air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline transportation. I challenge the Minister to find five people who are experts in all aspects of each mode.
Clause 5 of the Bill states that the Governor in Council should designate one member of the five to be chairman of the board. Here the Government is appointing five top-notch Canadians to this board and then telling them they are not competent enough to choose their own chairman, that the Minister will do it for them. Sure, the Minister will do it for them because then he will have the chairman in his pocket. That is the problem with the CASB. Mr. Justice Sopinka and the Canadian Bar Association challenged the Government on that clause of the Bill. Government Members are thanking everyone for input. Why do they not use some of that input?
Clauses 9 and 10 of the Bill provide that such employees as are necessary for the proper conduct of the work of the board shall be appointed in accordance with the Public Service Employment Act. That is just a nice way of saying that again the Minister will have a hand in selecting staff.
Under the title directors of investigations and other investigators it states:
10(1) From among the employees appointed under subsection 9(1)
there shall be -
The Bill does not clarify who appoints these directors of investigations. Will the power lie with the director of education and the chairman, bypassing the wishes of the members? When members ask for more information or ask that certain parts of an accident should be investigated further, will the chairman and director of investigation say: "Sorry, there is no need for it"? That happened in the Gander crash. This is why we are asking why the Government is rushing the Bill through. What is the Minister's hidden agenda?
April 17, 1989

I would like to compliment the Government on parts of the Bill. For example, I am pleased that the Government built in a review process. Section 63(1) states:
The Governor in Council shall, in January 1994, appoint one or more persons to carry out a comprehensive review of the operation of this Act for the purpose of assessing its effect on the safety of air-
That is a good recommendation with which we agree. If the Government feels that a review process is important in 1994, does it not feel that there should have been a review process on the Canadian aviation safety Bill? That is why we are suggesting that we should wait for Justice Estey's report.
Before Bill C-163, the CASB Bill, was implemented we had the investigations and the knowledge of Justice Dubin. That is why it was a good Bill. There are many things in that Bill that have to be ironed out, studied, changed, or amended.
When the Minister gave a background to the release of the Bill, he stated: "the Bill tabled today is much improved as a result of these extensive consultations over the past year. The Bill also clarifies the confusion which has arisen over interpretation of the CASB Act with regard to the roles and responsibilities of the chairman, board members, and investigators." This Bill does not clarify that. The confusion is still there, and the confusion will continue to plague the new Board just as the CASB was plagued with this confusion.
As I mentioned in one of my questions, one of the biggest errors that the Government has made in bringing forward the Bill is that it did not accept the recommendations of the Canadian Bar Association and Justice Sopinka. In the document entitled "Review of John Sopinka's Recommendations to the Minister of Transport" and the submission of the Canadian Bar Association to Transport Canada, it states: "The Government's failure to adopt recommendations from two of the most respected sources of legal opinion in Canada opens an avenue to raise serious questions. Many controversial and contradicting events have taken place at the CASB in recent times. These need no elaboration. Why has the Government chosen not to adopt provisions that would have corrected these and gone a long way toward improving transportation safety standards in Canada?"
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
The Official Opposition agrees with the intent of the Bill. However, we do not agree with the hidden agenda of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis). He makes much ado about the fact that all the recommendations from Justice Sopinka were not used. Nonetheless, a great many people were consulted about the legislation that we have before us today.
There was general recommendation made that it was good to separate the Board from the investigating arm itself so that the Board would function as a board to ask the correct questions of the investigators.
At the time Justice Sopinka was asked for his comments he was not a justice but a very highly respected lawyer. On Section 4 which provides for five members, Justice Sopinka stated that he agreed that the Board was too large. There should be at least one member from each mode of transportation so that at least one person with experience in each mode can be appointed.
For a five-member board the composition should be aviation, two; marine, one; railway, one; commodity pipeline, one; making a grand total of five. Therefore, it is false to give the impression today that we have not been listening to what Justice Sopinka has said. Certainly, all the recommendations of each individual person who reviewed the draft Bill were not followed. However, by and large the thrust of them were. I am glad to hear that both opposition Parties have at least said that the thrust of the Bill was in the right direction.

I still stick to what I said about not accepting the recommendations of Justice Sopinka and the Canadian Bar Association. That was already in the Bill, and it was not a recommendation from Justice John Sopinka.
I would like to answer the Member with a rhetorical question. How can a board of five be operated when all that is needed for a quorum is two members? Again, this Board of five members will have the same problems as the board of nine members under the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.

I am pleased to see the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Flis) back in the House after his sojourn. His contribution in a previous Parliament was notable.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member to respond to suggestions that the purview of the committee should be expanded somewhat. There is a definition in the aviation accident area that aircraft is too limited. There have been suggestions that sport parachuting should come under their purview. The ability to investigate accidents involving military aircraft doing aerobatic demonstrations in public areas, hang-gliders, and ultralights where there have been a number of deaths in Canada, is a regulatory vacuum area.
Would the Hon. Member like to comment on the example of sport parachuting where the government restraint program has wound up cutting the Canadian Sports Parachuting Organization out of the umbrella group? It has lost its funding and lost its technical adviser, making the sport somewhat more hazardous. Yet there is no over-all investigative body. How would the Hon. Member approach expanding that section to a little broader examination of safety questions?

I thank the Hon. Member for those kind comments. That is why it is always a pleasure to return to places like this.
The comments of the Hon. Member agree with what I have stated. The Government does not appear to have a commitment to safety in transportation. What can a captain who has been flying nothing but jumbo jets know about gliders? That sector of sports and transportation should be represented.
Is it represented in this Bill? No, Madam Speaker, it is not. This is something that we should raise in committee. I hope the Government does not attempt to bulldoze this Bill through committee as quickly as it is attempting to force it through the House.
I stress that we should be waiting for the recommendations and comments of Justice Estey. We should consider representations such as those we have heard from my colleague in the New Democratic Party.
We agree with the intent of the Bill, to make transportation safer. Let us work together in committee. That is why I enjoyed the transportation committee; when we got Out of this place we sort of put aside our partisanship politics and we tried to work together to improve a Bill.
Some Members of the House will recall that the Canadian Aviation Safety Bill went through quite quickly, but there was that agreement too. Let us see if a unimodal board will work. If it does, let us expand it to involve all modes of transportation. Maybe the Bill is okay. Maybe the Canadian Aviation Safety Board is okay. Maybe the fault lies in the incompetent Government opposite.

Madam Speaker, I have another question for the former Parliamentary Secretary who is knowledgeable in these areas. The problem is that the development of aviation safety is based on the Government responding to the recommendations of an accident investigation agency and the failure to do that because of cutting of personnel, cutting of budgets and basically almost leaving the private sector to handle many of these things.
I would like to make a suggestion that has been made to me, that the Transport Committee should immediately have the report of these agencies referred to it, that the Transport Committee should be monitoring the recommendations and the implementation of the recommendations, and that it should be required to present a report to the House of Commons on implementations of recommendations put forward by the safety agency.
How would the Hon. Member respond to that suggestion which has been brought forward on a couple of occasions, that monitoring must take place and a report to the House from one of its own agencies rather than the Public Service?

I think if that were implemented, Madam Speaker, what it would avoid is what happened in the Dryden crash where Air Ontario got the recommendations five days after the crash. I think we need a better watch-dog on transport matters, and what better watchdog than the Transport Committee.

ment, rather than a subsidiary group of an enormously large department.
There has been the suggestion made that this multimodal approach is almost going in a direction counter to where it should be going, that the problems of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board should be resolved by legislation and changes, and that a unimodal approach should be continued and enhanced rather than amalgamating it all into a very narrow board where they would have to compete internally for resources in each area and then go forward to the Ministry and to the Government to compete for a much smaller piece of the pie.
Is he familiar with the fact that there is talk of breaking the FAA out in the United States into a separate agency and allowing in Canada almost a move in the opposite direction of trying to integrate aviation and the other forms of transportation together in a much smaller body where they would be much more limited?

I thank the Hon. Member for the series of questions. I do not think that following trends that are happening across the border is always the correct direction to go. I think deregulation took place much faster in the United States than in Canada. We recommended deregulation. It was a limited regulation which we monitored to move slowly. Unfortunately, when this Government got in it just opened the doors and let the airline companies dictate regulations. This is why we have such a mess at Pearson and so on.
I think we are going in the right direction with a multimodal Board, but I think we have to make sure that we have more resources. I hope the Government does not think that it is going to try to operate a multimodal board with the same people resource and the same financial resources as they did for a unimodal board. I give the Minister at least that much credit for his thinking.
We can proceed in the direction we are going, but we should do it a little more slowly. I think we should wait for Justice Estey's recommendations. Maybe after we hear from him we may have to seek further information. Maybe we have to ask for a more in-depth inquiry such as the inquiry by Justice Dubin.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for North Island-Powell River.

Madam Speaker, it has been an interesting debate to this point in time. It certainly raises many questions in the House that
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
cause us all great concern. The whole question of safety in transportation is foremost on the minds of almost everybody in this country at the rate that we move here.
I am often surprised that highways are not the greatest national concern, considering the carnage and destruction on highways. Yet we as a national legislature pay very little attention to what causes the greatest number of deaths and injuries and destruction of property in this country. We spend an enormous amount of time on the others not without justification, but certainly it is always surprising.
I personally have misgivings about the Bill before us today. I think that by moving into a multimodal approach, especially with the experience that the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) referred to, there has not been great success with handling that approach and there is the suspicion that it is going to be there to submerge politically embarrassing issues rather than to serve the needs of safety.
Next, we should not lose sight that safety is a multifaceted thing, from the aviation point of view, the people who are involved in air regulation, air worthiness, personnel licensing, people involved in enforcement, air navigation, airports, all the way down the road. However, when something does go wrong in the system, the bottom line is the accident investigation group. They are the ones who take a look at the failure of the system, where it occurred. They examine it impartially, without finding blame but just to find out what went wrong, and then refer it back to those other safety agencies to rectify the situation.
Ultimately when there is an error in the system we cannot shy on the resources. When the Dubin commission started there was a profound belief that government was politically interfering with the results of aviation investigation, to the extent where it was suggested in this House, in committee, and in many other forums that the air administrator of the day was in fact rewriting the accident investigation reports when he did not like them, before submitting them to Parliament or to the public.
I think that day has changed considerably with the Canadian Aviation Safety Board and Justice Dubin's inquiry and recommendations, the attempt to give independence to that Board. Another about the Aviation Safety Board is that there really seems to be a severe problem of personalities in that the Board has not been able to take up the challenge and resolve the personality issues involved in it so that it can move forward over a couple of nasty accidents. We as legislators and Canadians should see it in the broader perspective that the

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
Board in its short growth period or period of adaptation in fact has done a good job over all.
It has handled hundreds if not thousands of cases without controversy, without problem. It has given good recommendations and in fact did the job. It certainly hit a major stumbling block with the Gander investigation. When it comes down to the bottom line we have to ask: Can it be expected to answer all the questions?
Out of the Gander investigation certainly procedural changes will follow. There may be new investigative techniques to create retrospectively a situation that will help us come forward with a solution. There were certainly security questions at the other end. Whether there was a bomb on that aircraft was not the issue, but certainly the security to stop the potential for it occurring was resolved.
Everyone involved in that Gander crash learned something about it. Indeed the Safety Board learned something about it as did those who investigated it. Unfortunately it probably means the end of that organization as a result.
There is a lot of concern about the name of the board. It should be called the transport safety board or something along that line to enhance the idea that the board is there to prevent accidents and to promote safety and that the bottom line accident investigation is about safety. The job is not only to investigate accidents. It is to investigate near misses and listen to suggetions that could in the future cause problems if not investigated.
We should be expanding the terms of reference of the Bill, particularly on the aviation side. Members of the Canadian Sport Parachute Association suggest that the Board should investigate parachute accidents because some of them have involved inferior, faulty equipment or not up-to-date equipment. The Board should be making recommendations so that operators are use up-to-date teaching techniques and the most advanced equipment to ensure safety in ultralights, hang-gliders or balloons. There is a whole host of things not strictly classed aircraft so we should have expansion of the Board's purview.
I come back to the parachute situation. The Government turfed the Canadian Sport Parachute Association out of the Fitness and Amateur Sport umbrella, cutting funding and, as I understand it, making sure that the organization could not continue to hire a technical advisor to make the sport safer. The direct result will be an unsafe situation with more fatalities.
I have mentioned the Transport Committee. There is a problem monitoring. If these boards continue to investigate accidents and make recommendations for implementation, who does the monitoring? The Minister through the Department of Transport authorizes monitoring. Information and implementation recommendations go to the Minister. If the Government is in a restraint mode, cutting personnel, resources and the budget, people will not hear about anything nor will they be able to raise the matter with the Government.
We should ensure that every report is referred to the Transport Committee to monitor the implementation of the recommendations. Thereafter the Transport Committee should be required to report to this House so that if the recommendations are not implemented there can at least be a public debate in a public forum about the lack of responsiveness toward it. Otherwise the whole system collapses. When there is an accident, the Board investigates and says the probability of having that accident occur again will be reduced by these changes. The Government says that they only happen once in a while and it is too expensive to implement so it will not do it right now, that no one can monitor that situation, but if the Transport Committee does it we would have a much safer situation. I urge the Committee to consider that suggestion.
Throughout the afternoon I have raised with a number of my colleagues in this House the problem of restraint being the major problem in transportation safety. On the one hand we have a conundrum which the Government has created by opening up access to promote transportation services through deregulation. There has been encouragement in the private sector to own and operate private aircraft. In centres like Toronto, and in Vancouver particularly, this expansion has created a nightmare because the Government has failed to put in the facilities required. Vancouver desperately needs a second runway. It needs air space reorganization. Vancouver is
April 17, 1989

about 20 to 40 controllers short, and Toronto is about 60 controllers short.
Toronto has had to modify procedures to make its runways safe because there are not enough controllers to do it. That is strictly restraint. The Government on the one hand asks everybody who wants to provide avaiation services to come in, and there has been a whole blossoming of new entrepreneurs in the aviation business. On the other hand the Government is not willing to provide the resources, namely air traffic controllers, air worthiness inspectors, maintenance people, adequate airport facilities, adequate navigation facilities, and adequate weather facilities. The Government is also talking about cutting a flight service station at Tofino. There is no other opportunity on the other side of the mountains on the west coast of Vancouver Island to get flight services, weather reports and some assistance if one is in difficulty. I urge the Government not to cut that service. Here is the great contradiction and it is time the Government woke up to it. If it is going to encourage a rapid, dramatic expansion in aviation as a result of deregulation, the Government must provide services and the resources to make sure the expansion is carried out safely.
This new multimodal Board is to be made up of five people. Many are saying the board membership is too small. I for one cannot see how a board that size can in any way give proper direction to four agencies-air, marine, rail and commodity pipelines. There are a number of aviation incidents, as I understand it, backlogged in the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. It does not have the resources to move them forward quickly enough to get the investigations done and the process out. We are looking at a far greater board with a potential for part-time members. When we talk about five people doing the task, it is impossible. Everything will be backlogged. If there is a single problem with a single accident and it is referred back, the whole system will be tied up.
There is also a problem with the Board in terms of competition for resources internally which could rip it to pieces, say the background of each of the board members, one from commodity pipeline, one from rail, marine, air and maybe the chairperson of the committee will double up with somebody else. It is a concern that
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
there will be disproportionate allocation of resources as louder voices get those resources. Fights will begin on the Board. There will be lack of agreements, and further personality breakdowns that we have seen with the present board. The Board should be bigger, and it should have the capacity to deal with reporting accident outcomes and recommendations in a timely way. With a board made up of five people there is a great deal of skepticism that this can take place. Is there a need to proceed right away on this issue?
The query by Mr. Justice Estey into the Gander accident will likely provide us with some excellent insights into the dilemmas faced by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. Once we have had an opportunity to look at that report, we will be in a better position to deal with this Bill. We have not had wide consultation on the Bill. The Bill has been changed. There are other people with lawyers looking at it who want to come forward with views. Since there is such a broad area of subject matter, we should move this Bill to committee now before giving approval in principle. We should allow the committee to take a look at the subject matter so that those who want to appear before the committee to make their points and proposals for changes to be made can do so.
If changes have to be made as a result of Mr. Justice Estey's report and as a result of the subject matter study, why can the Bill not then be brought back in, in a redrafted form, by the Government, given approval in principle, and moved quickly through to second reading? I agree with previous speakers that we should not be jamming this Bill through quickly.
Who will this committee report through? There was an indication in the speech of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), and I do hope it is the case, that he will not be the Minister of the Crown responsible for it. We hope it will be the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) or some other relevant Minister who takes the responsibility of reporting this to the House of Commons. The Board can then have the true appearance of an arms length situation and we do not have the suspicions that Transport is once again dabbling in the internal workings of the transportation safety system or the transportation accident investigation system. It is critically important that whichever Minister of the Crown reports to the

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
House, it not be the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard).
At this point, I would like to draw my remarks to a close. I think that the name of the board should be changed to the Safety Board, since that is what we are trying to enhance. The Minister of Transport should not be the one responsible for reporting this Bill to the House. It should be someone else, such as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis). I think the Transport Committee should be charged with the responsibility of monitoring the implementation of those recommendations, not for just receiving the report but having the responsibility for making a report to Parliament annually concerning the implementation of those safety recommendations.
With respect to the restraint program, the Government has to get its act together. There cannot be on the one hand unbridled deregulation and, on the other, the cutting of personnel budgets and services. That will make the situation a worse nightmare than it already is.
I return to the situation at Toronto Airport, which is about 60 controllers short. In Vancouver the situation will not resolve itself until after 1990. There is also a desperate need for a parallel runway there. I believe this is the only airport in Canada where there is an intersecting runway situation. Two airplanes can be cleared to land on the same runway and should both overshoot then the contract they have signed not to encroach on other people's runways becomes void. Two airplanes will fly at each other because of something that may have occurred on a runway. It is an absolutely ludicrous situation and potentially very dangerous. The airport has to be upgraded. The airspace has to be reorganized to make it an operationally safe place. The main point is that it needs the human and physical resources to carry that out.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to comment on the reference by my Hon. friend to the number of members on the Board. He said that five members was not enough. But it says in subsection (2) that the Governor in Council shall appoint as members five persons who are collectively knowledgeable about air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline transportation.
Fortunately, not many transportation accidents in Canada require an investigation of that caliber. And I wonder what the Hon. Member means when he says we
don't have enough members. How many people would he like to see on this Board, since we have people who are specialists in each field?

Madam Speaker, I am absolutely astounded by the Hon. Member's comment. First, there are thousands of accidents, incidents and occurrences. If someone does not investigate and draw a conclusion as to why they occur and then make recommendations for the situation to change we may find much larger and more serious accidents occurring. This board is not going to just look at accidents. I hope it will be looking at occurrences and incidents that have not become accidents.
As an example I refer to a near-miss between two jetliners. We must consider what created the situation. The potential is for 500 people to die if it reoccurs. We are not simply looking at accidents. Luckily, we do not have a large number of Ganders or Drydens. But we do have situations on almost a daily basis in cities like Vancouver and Toronto which, if they escalate, will have the potential for becoming major accidents. This is what I see the board becoming involved with.
I would see the number of members on the board being doubled. If we are looking at accidents or incidents involving rail, marine or air transportation, one good accident will likely take the single board member with the expertise in that area. What if we were to have something the same size as the oil spill at Valdez? That would be the end of our marine investigator for a good long time. What would then happen if there were another marine accident?
The point is, what if one of these people gets sick and the one with the key expertise is not able to be present throughout a major part of the investigation? Would the investigation be shelved? Would the person come back after the report is written and say: "You did this without my expertise. Therefore, I am not prepared to get on board and authenticate it"? An enormous great battle would occur afterward. So I say there are not enough people on the board. I think most people would like to see a larger number. Perhaps the number could be doubled to 10 so that there would be a back-up in the case of a large accident which would take a member of the board away. What will happen if a person gets ill or the backlog gets too heavy?
April 17, 1989

Madam Speaker, I have a few observations to make on the remarks of the Eton. Member. He mentioned restraint. He mentioned one member of the board not being available. But he failed to mention that there will be approximately 300 people employed by the board. There will not be just five people but 300. If one person is away I am sure it would not hurt the board too badly.
The Hon. Member urged the Government not to show restraint in this area. The Government will not be showing restraint in this area. There are approximately 300 people working in this field now and there will continue to be as many. There is no intent to decrease the number at all.
The Hon. Member brings up the too-fast, too-slow question. He says we are going too fast but we are going too stow all at the same time. I heard one Member say that we do not have good enough service and another saying we have too many airplanes in the air. It is a little confusing at times.
One thing that the Hon. Member did not mention is that we cannot stay with the status quo. Things are changing. Payloads are changing. Toxic wastes are changing. Volumes are changing. We cannot stay with the old legislation which addressed accidents in the old way. We have to have changes.
This Bill shows leadership. It provides for the necessary changes. There are no guarantees that it will be perfect. But in the legislation there is provision for the requirements to be reviewed after two years to see if they are operating properly. In January, 1995, there will be another review of operations under the Act. Those provisions are built into the Act, so I think it is quite safe.
The Hon. Member mentioned hang-gliders in his remarks. He feels they should come under transportation. That begs the question, should sailboards come under transportation, as well as bicycles and water slides? Perhaps the Hon. Member could answer those questions.

Madam Speaker, I am sorry that the Hon. Member has chosen to trivialize the issue. People have been killed. This is a national problem. In my remarks I came back several times to the parachute association and the deliberate pushing by the Government of that association out from under the fitness and amateur sports umbrella. The immediate response of the association was that it had to let its technical adviser go. Concerning the number of deaths we have had in Canada, people have said to me that if the correct technical advice were there and some mechanism existed to ensure that the operators used
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
modern techniques and equipment, then many deaths would be unnecessary. Anything that the Hon. Member says to trivialize that is unacceptable to me. I am sure he did not mean that.
When I talked about restraint I was not talking about restraint on the Aviation Safety Board or the Accident Investigation Board. What I was talking about is a Government that is criminally negligent by cutting back in its hiring of air traffic controllers for three years in an environment in which it deregulated aviation. We now find ourselves in a terrible situation in many airports, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver.
Someone said that a professional pilot and his family were in the plane that crashed in Dryden. As soon as the plane started off the runway this pitot said: "Put your heads down. This plane is going to crash". I would tell the Government, if we have to took forward to the same kind of management that we had in air transportation and the cuts that occurred between 1985 and 1988 with air traffic controllers and failing to address the problem of the parallel runways at Vancouver, then members of the Government ought to put their heads down because this system will crash.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Fontana).

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make some opening comments with respect to Bill C-2, introduced by the Government some two weeks ago, an Act to establish the Transportation Accident Investigation Board. I listened with great interest this morning to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard). His words were, I believe, laudable and sincere. He sang a good tune, but upon review of this proposed Bill, I am not sure he is singing from the same song sheet.
The public has tost confidence in this Government, its boards and agencies, especially as it relates to safety in the air, rail and seas of this country. Safety, safety, safety is on the minds of a confused and troubled public. We on this side for the past four months have spoken about air safety on a daily basis. I would agree that safety is and should be a non-partisan issue. Therefore, I hope this Government will have the political will to put in place a law that will in fact speak to safety for a multimodal transportation network in this country, and how to prevent accidents from occurring. We hope it will be a positive and a pro-active approach as opposed to reactive one, one that speaks of prevention, not only investigation. Changing the name of a board and the members of a board without giving it a clear, independent, responsi-

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
ble and accountable mandate will not stop one accident from occurring. We need a board that will have the opportunity of reviewing and investigating all aspects of our transportation safety systems, not only to investigate tragedies after the fact.
Safety speaks to preventing tragedies from occurring. Madam Speaker, my colleagues on this side of the House have addressed other concerns, but I wish to address some concerns with respect to Clause 7. It says the object of the Board is to advance transportation safety. It says:
(a)	by conducting independent investigations and, if necessary, public inquiries into transportation occurrences in order to make findings as to their causes and contributing factors;
(b)	by reporting publicly on its investigations and public inquiries and on the findings in relation thereto;
(c)	by identifying safety deficiencies as evidenced by transportation occurrences;
Madam Speaker, you will note that all of the objects of this speak to advancing transportation safety after the fact. This afternoon, the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) indicated a willingness for additional input before the Bill is enacted. The Minister of State for Transport indicated some positive input from various law societies and Chambers of Commerce. But what about the people on the front lines, the workers, the inspectors, the supervisors in our aviation, railroad and marine industries?
Madam Speaker, the most serious problems with the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act have not been addressed in the new proposed Accident Investigation Act. Strong recommendations by the Canadian Bar Association and Justice John Sopinka, which would have gone a long way to correct these problems, have been rejected and not incorporated into this retread of Bill C-142 which was introduced in July of 1988. The dissension, conflict of interest, the lack of independence are simply being transplanted into this proposed new board. So much for public input. Both the chairman and the director of investigation seem to have too much power in respect to the board, a board of only five members that must be knowledgeable on all aspects of air, rail, marine and pipeline.
We on this side of the House are prepared to work with the Government, but this new multimodal investigation agency must be of the highest standard, employing top Canadian experts and independent of the Minister. The public will not settle for anything less.
In July, 1988, the then Minister of Transport said:
The National Transportation Act places safety at the top of our
objectives. The Government takes this commitment seriously.
Since then, Canadians have witnessed incident after incident in our aviation industry and on our railroads. We still have shortages of air traffic controllers, a shortage of inspectors for aircraft and railroad rolling stock. The Government must not wait for this Act to be passed before putting in place those actions necessary to restore public confidence and public safety. Let us hope that this new board means more to the Government than merely a new name, a new face with an old mandate. Let us hope we are not replacing the board with a transportation czar that merely wants four rubber stamps for the Minister. We on this side of the House are prepared to take on the challenge of really coming to grips with all the real problems if the Minister and the Government are willing to do so. Thank you.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in listening to the Hon. Member and also the Member that spoke before him, much has been made about the name of the Bill by the word "safety". Really, the reason the Minister has not chosen to put the word safety into the Bill is because it would give a different connotation as to what the Board is all about. The name Transportation Accident and Investigation Board reflects more precisely what the principal activity of the board is in its investigation of accidents. The use of the name safety, such as Transportation Safety Board, would give the impression that the Board's mandate is actually wider than it really is.
The main objective of the board is investigation of accidents, and it is to make recommendations to improve transportation safety in all modes. The responsibility for implementing the improved safety regulations lies with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard). It is he, not the board, who is responsible for the safety and the regulations that go into that.

April 17, 1989

So why the Member keeps harping about the word safety having to be in the name is really sending out the wrong message. We want a board that will review what the investigators are doing, to make sure they have asked the right questions to make the recommendations to the Minister as to what regulations should be improved.
I am not sending the wrong message. In fact, I think the message that I and my Party are sending is that safety should come first.
Hear, hear!

If the Hon. Member is suggesting that the Minister of Transport is ultimately going to be responsible for all safety action in the air, on the railroads and on the seas, then I think that is really asking too much of the Minister. I heard the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) suggesting this afternoon that there has to be a separation between investigation and safety. I, and I believe our Party, do not agree with that position. I believe that prevention is where the Government should be going. This board should put its stock in prevention so that we can act before tragedies occur. Surely safety, prevention and investigation of those things that make a system unsafe should be something that this board should be looking into. I hope the board, and through the committees, we are able to develop a clear mandate so that the board can investigate accidents after the fact as opposed to being pro-active and looking at ways of preventing things from occurring because of bad safety practices of an agency or company.
Hear, hear!

I would like to ask the Member to respond to a comment that says regional safety officers of Transport Canada should in fact be moved out of Transport Canada and placed under the auspices of this board in order to continue the arm's length relationship between safety and some of the enforcement practices of Transport Canada. There have been suggestions that the safety officers could be more effective if they were seen, not as enforcement officers, but officers responsible for education in the promotion of safety. There is a bit of jading of the response. I would ask the Hon. Member how he feels about that. Secondly,
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
when they are talking about the mandate of the board, it is to deal with aviation occurrences, which is designated as any accident or incident involved in the operation of an aircraft.
It is contemplated that the Board will look at incidents, not just accidents, that can be used to develop and improve safety. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on whether the regional safety officers should be placed under the auspices of the Transportation Safety Board rather than Transport Canada.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member who spoke before me talked about prevention. Obviously, his idea of the regional officers being responsible or associated in a preventative way could be considered by the committee. That is a positive point we would consider.
I want to make a comment to him with respect to occurrences being defined as incidents. Let us be clear. If that is the intention of the Government, that is exactly what it should spell out as a clear mandate. The last thing we need is another board that is confused by its mandate and what it can or cannot do. If it is possible for it to investigate possible incidents or things that are brought to their attention by a railroad worker or someone in the industry who finds something unsafe, then let us be clear in the legislation. Let us put it in.
I believe he was talking about prevention. I think the board has to be much more than essentially an investigative arm of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard). I think it has to be pro-active and look for prevention.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member would examine the legislation he would see what the scope of the board's mandate really is. The board may exercise its mandate for any of the modes we talked about. It is free to decide the extent of any investigation and how different investigations will be conducted. It can decide, for example, if a public hearing is to be held on an issue. It will set the rules of how the investigation should be held and what should be taken.
When it comes to carrying out the recommendations to see that they have been followed, that is the responsibility of the Minister himself. The board is the one that carries out the responsibilities. It has the mandate. That is what is in the legislation.

April 17, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Board
The board has exclusive jurisdiction to investigate the transportation occurrences for any of the modes involved, marine, air, railway and commodities transported by pipeline.

Madam Speaker, I look forward to the Hon. Member's work on the committee, to essentially spell out what in fact he has indicated. I do not see that in the Bill. Perhaps there is a way of clarifying the issue.
I am sure that all Parties in the House have one mission, which is obviously to make safety paramount in the air, on the rails, on the seas and especially with respect to pipelines. If there is a way of clarifying that mission, that he believes the board has, then I and our Party are prepared to support it. Let us clarify it so there are no questions afterwards about what this board can or cannot do.
Question.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Unfortunately, I cannot recognize the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi) at this time. Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, the legislation before us today is very important. We know there have been a lot of problems under the existing board. There has been concern with regard to political interference as well as controversy with regard to how the board is working in relation to the staff. I am concerned that this legislation will not resolve any of those problems.
We know that there must be a competent board that can study the situation. We have to know that the people who are appointed to the board are not appointed because they happen to represent a certain region of Canada but have no knowledge about transportation.
My hon. friend, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), points out the fact that although they maybe Conservatives does not necessarily mean they are knowledgeable about transportation. Our former transport critic, the Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), correctly pointed out earlier today that having someone on the board who admits that their only knowledge about air transport is having taken some flights, does not give much security to Canadians.
I come from a riding where people in a number of my communities have no choice but to travel by air. There are no roads or rail lines and air transportation is then-only means of getting in and out of the communities. We know that as a result of deregulation, problems with air transportation increase daily. For example, Canadian Airlines International was supposed to have started its new schedule in my riding on April 2. It admits that it could not implement the schedule on time and, for that matter, has told us it would like to put the new schedule in place for May 2, one month later.
However, it cannot tell me when the planes will be flying to and from my riding. Canadian Airlines International is one of our two major airlines, responsible for flights right across the nation, but it does not even know when it will be flying into communities only two weeks from now.
How can there be any sense of confidence in our airlines when they cannot even plan their schedules as a result of this new climate of deregulation?
Last week our transportation critic released a number of documents in the House of Commons which show that it was known that deregulation would result in the same problems the Americans have experienced. The documents released by my colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), show that the industry and the department knew that safety would be threatened and that, as a result of trying to maintain their profits, maintenance would be an area where the airlines would cut back. That is happening now.
Canadians are very apprehensive about flying. They are very concerned about whether or not we have safety in the air. We hear about near misses at Pearson. We know that if you fly through Toronto you might as well add an extra hour or two to your day and perhaps miss your connecting flight.
We are in a situation where we know the Government has been cutting back. My community faces the same problem. It has been cutting back in renovations at airports and there are air strips maintained by the federal Government which have been unsafe for three or four years. The work has not been done.
A couple of years ago in my riding a PWA jet, as it was known then, could not land safely on the airstrip. That is what we are dealing with now.
April 17, 1989

I see it is six o'clock. If the Government calls this legislation for tomorrow, I will be glad to take my 18 and one-half minutes left to me at that time.
