subtopic: ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE-BILATERAL PROCESS
ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE-BILATERAL PROCESS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over the weekend most of the native students protesting against the Government's cut-back to native post-secondary education assistance ended their fast. The Government, more particularly the Minister responsible for Canada's Indian and Inuit people, can no longer put this matter off. It is time for the Government to stand up to its commitment of beginning a bilateral consultative process on the issue.
The Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) has repeatedly said he is committed to a bilateral consultative process with native leaders. He also said that he is prepared to meet with whoever wishes to discuss the cut-backs and that he is prepared to review the program as soon as the hunger strike ends. It is now up to the Minister to make the first move and to invite native leaders and students to meetings which will begin that process.
It is now time for the Government to show some leadership. It is now time for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to negotiate in good faith with the Indian people of Canada on the Native Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program. This must be a priority for the Minister.
Post-secondary education for our native peoples is the key to self-determination and economic self-reliance. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Cabinet have repeatedly said that the country's future is dependent upon economic development. Does this Government have one opinion for non-native people and a different one for native people?
There are 46 native communities in my riding. Many of them have very active economic development projects in
Adjournment Debate
the works which will ensure economic self-reliance in the years to come. Jobs have been created for the people. Welfare pay-outs have decreased. Drug and alcohol abuse is also on the decrease. These results have largely been achieved by people who have been through the post-secondary education system and have returned to their communities with the skills and knowledge to carry out these projects.
By restricting the number of students under the Native Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program, by limiting the funding by capping it at $130 million, and by removing incentives for masters and doctorate degrees, the Government has gone at least 10 years back in time. The changes in this policy will restrict the development of Canada's First Nations and will condemn many of them to continuing dependency on the Government from birth until death. Under this Government, Canada's First Nations people will not achieve self-determination and economic self-reliance. The Government has, in essence, put an end to many young native peoples' futures.
The success stories of the Native Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program are many. Indian and Inuit lawyers, doctors, teachers and administrators, to name just a few, have come through the system. Those who choose not to return to their communities pay taxes to the Government. Canada's native peoples want to make a contribution to society. They do not want hand-outs. They do not want to be totally dependent on the Government.
The Government knows full well that this issue is a long-standing one. Since it first announced its intentions to review the Native Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program in 1987, native peoples have been asking for a full bilateral review. Why has the Government waited until things got out of hand? Why has the Government announced changes to a policy without consulting the people it will most affect? Why must our First Nations resort to hunger strikes to get their message across? It is because this Government and the Minister of Indian Affairs have not been listening to native people.
A bureaucracy, concerned with its own future, is dictating the policies of the Government when it comes to native people. When will the Government learn from its mistakes?
Finally, 10 students have demonstrated their good faith by ending their fast. I call on the Minister of Indian Affairs to demonstrate his good faith by living up to his commitment and beginning immediately a bilateral con-

April 17, 1989
Adjournment Debate
sultative process with the First Nations people of Canada on the issue of native post-secondary education.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE-BILATERAL PROCESS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on April 14, 1989, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Nault), raised several concerns on which I wish to comment. The Government announced changes to the E-12 guidelines in May 1987 and indicated at that time that a process would begin to develop a new policy. An intensive consultation period began in July 1988 and concluded on December 31,1988. During this period, meetings were held with over 500 Indian groups and individuals. We received important and useful feedback which resulted in many changes to the draft which was circulated in 1988.
For example, up to 5 per cent of the students will be eligible for scholarships of $3,500 for successful study in a range of programs supporting self-government and economic development. As well, the new policy includes an annual scholarship of $1,000 based on academic achievement.
The Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program which the Government maintains for eligible Indian students is fair and generous. It provides assistance for a range of expenses which include tuition, living allowances, seasonal travel and books and supplies. Some 84 per cent of the students will obtain higher benefits under the new rates for living allowances.
Interest on the part of Indians in post-secondary education has increased steadily since 1964 when fewer than 170 Indians enrolled in university. The program budget reflects these increases. In a letter to the chiefs and councils of March 20, 1989, the Minister indicated that the budget for the program rose from $9 million in 1977-78 to close to $130 million in 1988-89.
The Government is committed to Indian post-secondary education. We have a generous student assistance program already in place. Should an Indian student's application be deferred, it would be given top priority the following year. In such a case, this student, like any other Canadian student, would have access to the Canada Student Loan Program to help offset expenses. In addition, if this student qualifies, there are provincially administered student loan programs and university and college scholarships and bursaries available. Access to a post-secondary education for eligible Indian students is therefore clearly not in question.
In conclusion, the Minister will be meeting in the near future with the chiefs and the students who have ceased their fasting in order to seek resolutions to the concerns raised.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS-WHITE PAPER-REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS-WHITE PAPER-REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope I receive a better answer to my question than the one that was just given to my hon. colleague from Kenora-Rainy River. It is interesting to note that very often Parliamentary Secretaries come into the House and give an answer without even listening to what the Hon. Member has said. They read out answers prepared by bureaucrats in the Departments.
On Friday, April 14,1 continued to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) questions with respect to changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which she announced on Tuesday, April 11. On that date, the Minister announced that she was redirecting $1.3 billion from the unemployment insurance fund to other programs. In other words, she was taking money away from a fund contributed to by workers and employers to protect the workers who are put out of work against their will.
Of that money $450 million was redirected to improvements in the Unemployment Insurance Act and we do not have much complaint with that. These are improvements with respect to parental benefits, senior worker benefits, and benefits for persons involved in labour disputes. However, we do not give much credit to the Government for that because the courts of Canada have all ruled that those benefits must be covered. Even though the Government made appeals to higher courts to contest those rulings, it has now seen the light and is covering those things. That is good and we have no disagreement with that.
With respect to $850 million that is being redirected to such things as training, labour resource planning, consultation, apprenticeship and co-operative education, we feel that although these are all good things which should be financed and improved, they should not be financed with moneys from the unemployment insurance fund. This is a new use of unemployment insurance moneys and we object to the use of these funds for these purposes. This is a regressive and inequitable way of funding programs which benefit all Canadians.
April 17, 1989

The programs that are being funded out of the unemployment insurance moneys do not just benefit the unemployed, they benefit the economy in general. To use unemployment insurance moneys is unfair because it reduces the money available to people who are unemployed and will cover people who have not even paid into the fund.
For example, the program will cover apprenticeship programs, co-operative education programs and entry programs, all of which are excellent programs. However, why should workers who have been paying for years into a fund to cover themselves for unemployment pay for those programs?
This is where there is some misunderstanding. Right now, unemployment insurance moneys are used for training programs but in order to qualify for those training programs, one must be a claimant under the unemployment insurance program, a beneficiary of the unemployment insurance program. Under the new proposals, one would never have to have contributed at all but would still qualify for those programs. We say that these proposals are wrong because labour-intensive industries will subsidize high-tech industries and underdeveloped regions of the country will subsidize developed regions, unless it precisely states in the legislation, which is the question I asked on Friday, that those moneys for training must go to the provinces and the regions where workers paid into the funds and that is not left to the discretion of the Minister.
We also oppose the program because through their contributions workers in low-skilled service industries will be paying to train high-skilled workers.
We object to this program and we want to receive some answers. All last week we asked questions, and today we asked questions. We are not receiving any answers from the Minister with respect to these issues.
I also want to know from the parliamentary secretary why the Minister has now announced that she is going to launch herself on a tour of the country to sell these programs. When I asked her on Friday to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, in order that parliamentarians from all Parties can also consult with the people
Adjournment Debate
throughout the country, the Minister said: "No, wait for the legislation". The Minister is not waiting for the legislation. She is going to be out there using taxpayers' money selling this program to the people in the country. If we are to be fair about this, parliamentarians in the Standing Committee should also be out in the country consulting with the people in the regions who will be affected. I want to hear some answers from the Government.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS-WHITE PAPER-REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member will be delighted to know that he is going to receive just as good an answer this time as he did the last time.
I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) on April 14 last.
On April 11, the Minister tabled a policy paper outlining a major federal government initiative of labour force development and unemployment insurance program.
The highlights include proposals to increase assistance to employers for human resource planning, special help to displaced older workers, more job related training for young people, and more generous benefits for both new parents and workers aged 65 and over. These measures will be financed through a reallocation of resources in the UI program.
A particularly important feature of the strategy is the increased role which is accorded to employer and employee organizations in government decision making about labour force programs.
The objective of the Government is to mobilize a national effort and to challenge Canadian business, unions, provincial and territorial Governments, educators, interested groups, and individual Canadians to give priority to increasing the skills levels of Canadians and finding the best combination of policies, programs, and employment practices to ensure that all Canadians can achieve their potential.
I can assure the House that the combined resources of the UI program and the Canadian Jobs Strategy will be

April 17, 1989
Adjournment Debate
maintained and used more effectively to help the Canadian unemployed.
The views of Canadians on the new labour force programs will be sought, and their suggestions will influence the final design of these measures. The labour force development strategy is designed to achieve four goals: a substantial increase in the private sector's role in training workers and in ensuring that training is more responsive to current labour market needs; a realignment within the UI program so that more expenditures are directed to active training and re-employment measures for the unemployed; in compliance with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, a significant improvement to UI benefits, to better respond to the needs of working parents and to encourage the full participation of those workers over 65; and a reduction of work disincentives that are currently in the UI program.
The Government intends to launch a major consultation effort in all parts of the country before implementing the new training programs. Our goal is to take the advice of those who have the greatest interest in the design of training programs, namely, Canadian employees and employers. This process will commence immediately and will continue for the next several months.
The size of the unemployment insurance program will not change, but the benefits available under UI will improve. More unemployed Canadians in all parts of Canada who need training to find good jobs will be able to use their UI benefits while they are on training.
I can assure the Elon. Member that the $800 million in redirected funds will improve the employment prospects of unemployed Canadians in each and every region of the country.

subtopic: ENERGY-ENERGY ALTERNATIVE PROGRAMS-TERMINATION OF POSITIONS-ALTERNATIVE ENERGY DEVELOPMENT
ENERGY-ENERGY ALTERNATIVE PROGRAMS-TERMINATION OF POSITIONS-ALTERNATIVE ENERGY DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot cover a lot of ground in a few minutes this evening, however I would like to pose some questions to the Government on energy conservation, alternative energy, and developing a more environmentally sustainable energy future.
There is no doubt that more Canadians than ever before are concerned about protecting the environment. They listened carefully when the Brundtland commission called for major changes to ensure that the environment and economic development are seen as two sides of the same coin. They have followed reports about the damage to the ozone layer, and they take note when scientists advocate sharp reductions in the emissions of carbon dioxide to tackle the greenhouse effect.
The more visible and spectacular environmental disasters, such as the PCB fire in Quebec, and the recent oil spills off the west coast, have only reinforced the public's already deep-seated and justifiable concerns about the environment.
By contrast, it seems fair to say that Canada's Government has lagged far, far behind ordinary Canadians and is now scrambling to catch up with public opinion. There is still a huge gap between what the Government says and what it does. The Government's words indicate that it is aware that Canadians are concerned about the environment.
The Government supported the goal of sustainable economic development. The previous Minister of the Environment called for a "fundamental shift in attitudes and practices at all levels". The current Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) made a brave start by stating that his Department would conduct environmental audits of previously approved projects. The Government's recent Throne Speech spoke of "the environmental imperative", stating that we face "an environmental challenge of unprecedented magnitude" and must strike a "new environmental agenda".
It would seem that on the whole the Government is saying a lot of the right things. However, Canadians are sophisticated and they know that actions speak louder than words. They are interested in looking beyond words to examine what lies behind all the rhetoric.
What does lie behind the rhetoric? Let us look at the evidence from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, where a great deal of valuable work on conservation and energy alternatives has been done in the past. What one discovers is a distressing list of program cuts. What are these cuts? I will give a sample. A listing of others is available in a background paper that I have prepared for anyone who wants one. I would cheerfully hand over to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary a copy for himself and for the Minister.
What did the Government cut? CHIP helped three million families upgrade the thermal efficiency of their homes. It was terminated in 1986. The Canada Energy Audit Program provided help for low cost changes to conserve energy. It was ended in 1986. This Solar Energy
April 17, 1989

Demonstration Program to develop cost effective applications of active solar energy ended this year. The Remote Community Demonstration Program to provide energy saving advice and financial support to 370 remote communities ended two weeks ago on March 31. The Forest Industry Renewable Energy Program to encourage biomass energy facilities, similarly shut down on March 31. All of those programs and more are gone.
Spending on energy conservation and alternative energy programs declined from $400 million per year in 1980-1984, to $150 million per year in 1985-1987, to only $50 million per year today.
This leads to my first question: What conclusion can Canadians reasonably draw from these massive cuts and the Government's public announcements other than that this Government's main intention is not to tackle today's environmental problems in a meaningful way but rather to conduct a successful public relations exercise merely to try to give Canadians the impression that it takes environmental concerns seriously?
On a more positive note, let us look to the future. When it comes to protecting the environment hundreds of energy related initiatives, low-tech, cheap, easy and effective initiatives, are just crying out for attention. The way to start is clearly by conserving energy. For example, encouraging the use of compact fluorescent lights in the ceilings of public plazas reduces electricity costs by approximately $70 per year and can reduce the need to bum coal and the subsequent emissions of SO2 and CO2. High efficiency refrigerators can save approximately $30 per year in electricity charges and can cut coal consumption and consequent CO2 and SO2 emissions. R-2000 super energy efficient houses with heat recovery ventilators can cut heating bills in half. Promoting the use of the many alternative energy sources is another area for progress.
Examples include developing the ethanol fuel industry in Canada, using com, and barley. Other agricultural products and forestry by-products would complement our fossil fuel sources and would provide jobs and much needed economic development in rural areas from the Maritimes to the Pacific. A recent U.S. Congressional study shows that 10 per cent ethanol blended gasoline would also reduce CO2 emissions.
Another example is actively promoting wind power in Atlantic Canada and in southern Alberta, particularly where the wind streams off the mountains. This simply
Adjournment Debate
makes good sense. As a special House of Commons committed on alternative energy pointed out in 1980, the possibilities for alternative energy sources are huge- heat pumps, hydrogen, and photovoltaics. We need not wait in the hope that desk-top fusion will provide yet another technological fix. We should proceed, with vision and commitment to our environment, to make some of these possibilities a reality.
This brings me to my second question: What new programs has the Government formulated, or is now formulating, to replace the massive cuts this Government has made to the energy conservation and alternative energy programs in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources?
Finally, since my time has all but expired: What plan of action has the Government devised to promote environmentally sustainable energy development in Canada? If no plan currently exists, what concrete steps have been taken to develop one in the near future?
I reminded the Government that Canadians are watching and waiting for substantive answers to these important questions and for action. They do not want even further evidence of inaction or confirmation of their suspicions that this Government is only trying to give the impression of caring about the future of our planet and that that suspicion is unfortunately correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-ENERGY ALTERNATIVE PROGRAMS-TERMINATION OF POSITIONS-ALTERNATIVE ENERGY DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to welcome the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) in his role as critic for the NDP. After his few comments, I imagine over the next period of time there will be quite a few evenings that we will be here together.
Given the recent round of publicity on this issue, I am pleased to be given the opportunity to clarify some of the misinformation that is being perpetrated by various reports. I would like to reiterate a point made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) when he initially responded to the Hon. Member in the House in last week's Question Period on Thursday, that is, that these resource deductions are nothing new. They were announced back in 1985 in an Energy, Mines and Resources planning document entitled "A Multi-Year Operational Plan" which projected reducing resource requirements to the year 1991, given the Government's move away from the costly energy conservation and renewable energy programs announced under the for-

April 17, 1989

mer Liberal Government's extravagant National Energy Program.
In September 1988 the Government announced the Energy Efficiency and Diversification Initiative Program in support of energy conservation, renewable energy, and alternative fuels for transportation.
The primary objectives of the EED are to enhance Canadian industrial competitiveness, physical environment, quality of life, and energy security throughout the promotion of efficiency and the energy consumption and diversification of energy sources and technology.
The EED is designed to address the kinds of energy and environment issues raised recently in the press and by various Members of the House. The EED initiative is clearly consistent with this Government's commitment to the environment. I make that very clear, Madam Speaker. It is an important energy policy initiative which we feel is a key part of the solution of these problems.
Unlike the programs under the former Liberal Government, EED is based on the principle of co-operation with the industry and the provinces. EED is not a rich giveaway program like that of the notorious National Energy Program. Instead, under the EED we are working closely with the industry and the provincial representatives to obtain a maximum leverage on the EED's
dollars. The emphasis under EED is on supporting research and development on energy efficiency and alternative energy and technology for the type that will be critical to dealing with the many environmental problems.
With the current EED which constitutes and focuses on the programs from the old regime there is no longer a need for as many employees to be involved in the administrative work and such matters. Instead, the EED ensures that Energy, Mines and Resources will retain a strong in-house technical capacity in the important areas of alternative energy which in turn will be an important part of the Government's many environmental initiatives.
This Government, this Minister, and every one of us in this House are concerned about the environment. In our Department we will ensure that environment is a very high priority.
